Overview and scope
In semi-arid cropping systems of the Northern Great Plains (NGP), agrobiodiversity can be operationalized through crop rotation complexity (adding pulses, oilseeds, forages; replacing summer fallow; varying sequence length and diversity), cover crop-based rotations, and intercropping (e.g., nurse crops like legumes with cereals, or cereal–pulse strips). Direct “recovery from shocks” evidence typically comes from multi-year field observations linking yields to rainfall variability, disturbance treatments (termination, rain events), and stand/vigor responses after stress; proxy indicators include pollinator abundance and soil carbon. Below, we synthesize which interventions have direct recovery/stability evidence versus proxy-supported claims, and the mechanisms validated under actual disturbance.

Interventions with direct shock-recovery evidence
Crop rotation complexity and fallow replacement
- Replacing wheat–sorghum–fallow with diversified rotations has been widely adopted in the High Plains/NGP in response to drought volatility; economic and environmental analyses attribute intensification/ diversification (e.g., adding pulses, oilseeds, sorghum, and reduced tillage) to improved water storage, reduced erosion, and risk management under highly variable weather, even though dryland corn retains high reproductive drought vulnerability and thus remains risky in some seasons.<cite id="02e393cf-2">Our results suggest there are high rates of cropping system intensification and diversification, even in the volatile and dry climate of the High Plains… since 2008, the dominant dryland cropping system by land area changed from wheat-fallow to mid-intensity rotations… transitions to continuous cropping have been linked to the emerging soil health movement… improved access to markets and local infrastructure for processing is a key driver of increases in sorghum and pea adoption… However, corn remains one of the more risky crops in dryland rotations under the highly variable weather conditions experienced in this region due to its high vulnerability to drought during reproduction.</cite> <cite id="02e393cf-3">Use of rotations with a fallow period has evolved as a means of increasing the likelihood of success dryland crop production in semi-arid regions, because rain in the fallow period is stored as soil moisture for a future crop… A 3-year rotation of wheat-sorghum-fallow has been found to be successful… success depends on an understanding of the regional rain events, and crop and soil management practices that can be used to increase storage of the rain that falls during these fallow periods… practices that minimize runoff and evaporation will tend to maximize soil water storage.</cite>
- Direct multi-year field evidence from NGP cover-crop trials shows that replacing fallow with cover mixes can depress following wheat yields in dry years, but in-season rainfall explains most of the yield variability, and termination timing/type (early vs late) modulates risks; these results imply stability is contingent on hydroclimate and management rather than an automatic monotonic improvement, with warm-season cover phases less water-intensive and sometimes safer for subsequent wheat.<cite id="39250078-1">The adoption of cover crops in replacement of fallow has been slow in the Northern Great Plains despite government incentives… Reductions in wheat yields following cover crops were frequent enough and important enough to raise some concerns… However, the previous year cover crop biomass was a poor predictor of wheat yields, whereas in-season rainfall explained more variability in wheat yields… Termination treatments did not significantly impact grain yield, soil nitrate or soil organic matter.</cite> <cite id="39250078-2">Reductions in wheat yields following cover crops as a replacement of fallow were frequent… maximum reductions were 1.4 t ha−1 (60%) for winter wheat and 1.1 t ha−1 (35%) for spring wheat… our data suggested that warm-season crops may limit the effect on subsequent wheat yields and be a safer alternative, possibly due to lower water use during the cover crop phase… crop failures in these mixtures in 2012 and 2017, and the low biomass accumulation generally, demonstrated a poor performance as cover.</cite>
- Rotation diversification that includes pulses reduces dependence on fallow and mitigates N and water limitations; field pea after wheat increases spring wheat yields and protein compared with wheat–wheat, and diversification has been associated with reduced crop failure risk, enhanced biodiversity, improved soil fertility, and higher farm income in dryland NGP contexts, consistent with mechanisms of N carryover and moisture retention from shorter-season legumes.<cite id="02e393cf-4">There is a need to include alternative crops in rotation with wheat in dryland cropping systems to diversify crop production and eliminate summer fallow… Studies have reported that spring wheat grain yield and protein increased following pulse crops compared to spring wheat following spring wheat… diversified rotations not only increased crop yields, but also reduced the risk of crop failure, enhanced biodiversity, improved soil fertility, and increased farm income… field peas require less water… and provide the opportunity to leave moisture in the soil profile after harvest.</cite>

Intercropping and nurse-crop strategies
- Nurse-cropping cereals with legumes is widely practiced in semi-arid Africa and serves multiple agrobiodiversity functions (nitrogen fixation, complementary light/radiation use, weed suppression), with reported maize benefits from residual N transfer and sometimes yields equal or higher than monoculture under certain conditions; however, at high legume densities sorghum yields can decrease, showing trade-offs that depend on spacing and resource partitioning under drought stress.<cite id="f78bb409-2">Intercropping is advantageous in terms of nutrition, biodiversity, and productivity… cowpea acts as a fertilizer due to its nitrogen-fixing capabilities… Residual nitrogen transfer in subsequent cropping cycles can increase maize yield up to 66% after 2 years of intercropping, in contrast to monocropping… However, under fertilized conditions, maize yield was lower in intercropped systems compared to mono-cropped systems… due to greater competition between the crops.</cite> <cite id="f78bb409-4">Cereal-legume intercropping… often has advantages over sole cropping in terms of improved crop productivity, land sustainability… combined grain yield… higher by 20–67% compared with sole crops… attributed to efficient utilization of water, radiation, and nutrients… a study in arid and semi-arid lands reported a decrease in sorghum yield at higher cowpea density.</cite>
- In semi-arid Zimbabwe, the performance of maize–legume intercropping versus monocultures varies seasonally with rainfall, with relay planting of legumes used to reduce early competition and harness legume drought tolerance; this operationalizes risk-sharing across years and rain years, aligning with direct stability logic under rainfall variability even when inter-season productivity trade-offs occur.<cite id="f78bb409-1">Seasonal rainfall impacts the relative performance of maize-legume intercropping systems in semi-arid Zimbabwe… planting basins harvest rainfall and conserve soil moisture… legume intercrops were relay planted 2–4 weeks after maize to reduce competition… Depending on rainfall availability…</cite>
- Although a classic study from semi-arid West Africa reported lower component yields in maize–cowpea intercropping yet higher land equivalent ratios (LER > 1.5), it underscores that intercropping can increase total land productivity without guaranteeing absolute component recovery under every drought shock; management (maize height/vegetative vigor) modulates the balance of risks and gains.<cite id="f78bb409-0">Intercropped cowpea yields were decreased by 29 and 26% and maize yields by 11 and 33% in short vs tall maize varieties across two seasons… Land equivalent ratio was greater with the shorter maize variety and with intercrops vs monocultures (1.51 vs 1.00)… although intercropping may result in decreases in the yield of one or both component crops, the productivity of a unit land area is higher with intercropping than with monoculture.</cite>

Mechanisms empirically validated under disturbance
- Water storage and runoff interception: In semi-arid dryland rotations, fallow and cover phases store rainwater for subsequent crops; practices that minimize runoff and evaporation (e.g., residue and no/low tillage) increase soil water storage during brief rain pulses, providing a buffer that stabilizes yields across dry and wet years.<cite id="02e393cf-3">Use of rotations with a fallow period… rain in the fallow period is stored as soil moisture for a future crop… practices that minimize runoff and evaporation from the soil will tend to maximize soil water storage during the fallow periods.</cite> <cite id="02e393cf-4">Field peas require less water… and provide the opportunity to leave moisture in the soil profile after harvest.</cite> <cite id="39250078-1">Termination treatments did not significantly impact grain yield… whereas in-season rainfall explained more variability in wheat yields.</cite>
- Resource partitioning and complementarity: Cereal–legume mixtures intercrop exploit different light, water, and nutrient niches, increasing radiation use efficiency and drought tolerance via complementary rooting and N acquisition; under semi-arid conditions, relay or spacing strategies reduce early-season competition to protect cereal establishment and leverage legume heat/drought tolerance for residual benefits and risk sharing across seasons.<cite id="f78bb409-2">Combining maize and cowpeas… use of different nitrogen sources… cowpea acts as a fertilizer due to nitrogen-fixing capabilities… residual nitrogen transfer in subsequent cropping cycles can increase maize yield…</cite> <cite id="f78bb409-4">An earlier study… combined grain yield of cereal and legumes was higher by 20–67%… attributed to efficient utilization of water, radiation, and nutrients in crop mixtures.</cite> <cite id="f78bb409-1">Planting basins harvest rainfall and conserve soil moisture… relay planting… to reduce competition with maize.</cite>
- Soil surface stabilization and early regrowth: In NGP cover-crop systems, termination timing modulates the risk window for subsequent wheat; early-terminated warm-season covers reduce transpiration demand and avoid biomass losses that could compromise moisture for the next crop, while late termination can build surface cover that reduces crusting and aids emergence after dry spells—mechanisms directly tied to observed yield responses to rainfall and termination rather than to soil C per se.<cite id="39250078-2">Warm-season crops may limit the effect on subsequent wheat yields and be a safer alternative, possibly due to lower water use during the cover crop phase… crop failures in these mixtures… demonstrated a poor performance as cover… low biomass and inconsistent cover… suggest that such low productivity and lack of consistent cover would not deliver expected soil health benefits over the long term.</cite> <cite id="39250078-1">Termination treatments did not significantly impact grain yield… but rainfall explained more variability… suggesting cover effects act through water management and planting conditions rather than bulk soil properties.</cite>

Interventions supported by proxy indicators with weaker direct shock-recovery validation
- Soil carbon and “health” proxies: In the NGP dryland context, replacing fallow with cover crops did not significantly change soil nitrate or soil organic matter over the study period even as wheat yields varied with rainfall, cautioning that soil C increases may lag or be insufficient to guarantee drought recovery; management decisions (e.g., termination timing) and hydroclimate dominate short-term yield stability, so relying solely on soil C accrual as a proxy for drought resilience can be misleading in semi-arid rotations.<cite id="39250078-1">Termination treatments did not significantly impact soil nitrate or soil organic matter… whereas in-season rainfall explained more variability in wheat yields.</cite> <cite id="02e393cf-4">Summer fallow usually retains soil water and nitrogen for the subsequent crop… however, wheat-fallow systems adversely affect soil quality by increasing erosion, reducing soil organic matter, and increasing nutrient loss… Therefore, there is a need to include alternative crops in rotation to diversify and eliminate summer fallow.</cite>
- Pollinator-focused biodiversity: While pulses benefit from biological nitrogen fixation and can be pollinator-reliant for seed production, NGP dryland small grains and dual-purpose forages often rely on cleistogamous or wind-pollinated processes, and direct field evidence linking pollinator abundance to drought-year yield insurance in these systems is thin compared to the direct rainfall/termination-based recovery evidence summarized above; thus, pollinator counts are a stronger conceptual proxy than an empirically validated drought-recovery metric in NGP cereals/forages.<cite id="02e393cf-4">Field pea is an important pulse crop that can be added to existing crop rotations to sustain crop yields in arid and semi-arid regions… Studies have reported that spring wheat grain yield and protein increased following pulse crops… diversified rotations… enhanced biodiversity…</cite> <cite id="39250078-1">Adoption concerns about cover crops in semi-arid systems were driven by observed wheat yield reductions, with rainfall rather than cover biomass predicting yield—highlighting hydroclimate over pollinator-mediated processes as the dominant short-term stability driver.</cite>

Mechanistic contrasts: proxy vs direct
- Deep rooting and mycorrhizal P cycling: In semi-arid rangelands and perennial forrests adjacent to cropland, deep-rooted species and mycorrhizal networks are repeatedly implicated in drought recovery via access to deeper water and remobilization of P; while these mechanisms underpin many agroecosystem proposals for dryland rotations (including medic/alfalfa in NGP pastures), direct field evidence tying these processes to dryland small-grain yield recovery in the NGP is less explicit than cover-driven water storage and pulse N carryover effects. The NGP cover-crop and rotation evidence shows immediate hydrologic and N mechanisms with measurable multi-year stability trade-offs, whereas deep-rooting/mycorrhizal mechanisms require longer-term or potometer/PLFA tracer studies to validate under actual disturbance windows.<cite id="02e393cf-3">Practices that minimize runoff and evaporation maximize soil water storage during fallow periods… A 3-year rotation of wheat-sorghum-fallow has been successful…</cite> <cite id="02e393cf-4">Field peas… leave moisture in the soil profile after harvest… diversified rotations reduced risk of crop failure and enhanced biodiversity.</cite>
- Residue/crusted-surface management: Direct observations from NGP cover-crop systems indicate that cover residues intercepted rain and reduced runoff/evaporation, but when cover biomass was low or terminated early, benefits diminished and wheat yields responded strongly to subsequent rainfall timing and amounts; this operationalizes the mechanism that residue-mediated surface stabilization and early-season regrowth after rain are primary routes of shock recovery in dryland rotations, rather than bulk SOC per se.<cite id="39250078-2">Low biomass accumulation and inconsistent cover demonstrated poor performance as a mulch, suggesting limited interception and infiltration benefits… warm-season covers may be safer due to lower water use, preserving moisture for following wheat.</cite> <cite id="39250078-1">In-season rainfall explained more variability in wheat yields than prior-year cover biomass, implying direct hydrologic coupling rather than slow SOC-mediated recovery.</cite>

What mechanisms are empirically validated under actual disturbance?
- Water interception and storage: Across semi-arid rotations and cover-crop systems in the NGP and adjacent regions, management that reduces runoff/evaporation and stores rainwater for subsequent crops is repeatedly validated as the primary mechanism for yield stability and post-shock recovery, with quantitative links between rainfall events and wheat yield variability and with practical guidance on termination timing to preserve stored moisture.<cite id="02e393cf-3">Practices that minimize runoff and evaporation will tend to maximize soil water storage during the fallow periods.</cite> <cite id="39250078-1">In-season rainfall explained more variability in wheat yields… suggesting direct hydrologic coupling.</cite>
- Nitrogen and moisture carryover: Pulse inclusion in rotations transfers fixed N to subsequent cereals and leaves moisture in the profile, reducing early-season N limitation and drought vulnerability; multi-year dryland studies report increased wheat yields and protein after peas and reduced crop failure risk, consistent with these mechanisms under actual yield shocks and sequence disturbances.<cite id="02e393cf-4">Field pea… provides the opportunity to leave moisture in the soil profile after harvest… spring wheat grain yield and protein increased following pulse crops… diversified rotations reduced the risk of crop failure…</cite>
- Competition trade-offs and relay timing: Intercropping and nurse crops validate complementary rooting and light capture with tactical relay timing to reduce early stress, evidenced by stability under rainfall variability where intercropping maintains land productivity and, in some cases, boosts component crop recovery across seasons via residual N and drought-tolerant nurse crops; however, high-density legumes can suppress cereals, underscoring the need for spatial/temporal partitioning under drought.<cite id="f78bb409-2">Residual nitrogen transfer… increased maize yield up to 66% after 2 years… cowpea acts as a fertilizer due to nitrogen-fixing capabilities.</cite> <cite id="f78bb409-4">Cereal–legume intercropping… attributed to efficient utilization of water, radiation, and nutrients… but higher legume density decreased sorghum yield in ASALs.</cite> <cite id="f78bb409-1">Seasonal rainfall impacts relative performance… relay planting 2–4 weeks after maize to reduce competition.</cite>
- Management buffering via cover termination and diversity: Empirical NGP field work shows that selecting warm-season cover phases and timely termination (to minimize water extraction) and diversifying rotations (adding pulses/oilseeds/forages) directly modulate the risk and magnitude of yield penalties in dry years, demonstrating mechanistic buffering of hydroclimatic shocks through water-use phenology and species pools in the rotation sequence.<cite id="39250078-2">Warm-season crops may limit the effect on subsequent wheat yields and be a safer alternative, possibly due to lower water use during the cover crop phase… crop failures in 2012 and 2017… low biomass accumulation generally.</cite> <cite id="02e393cf-2">Shift from wheat-fallow to mid-intensity rotations… enabled by soil health practices and drought-resistant varieties… increased yields while using fewer inputs, while acknowledging drought vulnerability during reproduction in corn.</cite>

Which interventions have direct recovery evidence versus proxies in the NGP and semi-arid systems?
- Directly evidenced to enhance stability/recovery:
  - Diversified rotations replacing fallow (including pulses/oilseeds/forages) that store water, reduce erosion, and increase N carryover; multi-year NGP studies show yield stability tracks rainfall and rotation water-use phenology rather than aggregate soil carbon, with pea following wheat increasing wheat yields and protein and reducing failure risk.<cite id="02e393cf-3">Rotations with fallow store rainwater for subsequent crops… practices that minimize runoff and evaporation increase storage.</cite> <cite id="02e393cf-4">Field pea addition… increased spring wheat yields and protein… diversified rotations reduced crop failure risk and enhanced biodiversity.</cite> <cite id="39250078-1">In-season rainfall explained wheat yield variability better than cover biomass; termination did not significantly impact yield or soil nitrate/soil organic matter.</cite>
  - Intercropping with nurse legumes (maize–cowpea, sorghum–cowpea), which maintains or increases land productivity and leverages complementary resource use and residual N; under semi-arid rainfall regimes, relay timing and plant height management modulate competition and early-season drought risk, providing stability through complementary physiology and risk diversification across years and rain events.<cite id="f78bb409-0">Intercrops showed LER > 1.5 vs monocultures despite lower component yields, showing higher land productivity.</cite> <cite id="f78bb409-2">Residual N transfer increased maize yield up to 66% after 2 years; cowpea fixes N and reduces competition via different N sources.</cite> <cite id="f78bb409-1">Seasonal rainfall impacts performance; relay planting reduces competition and conserves moisture.</cite>
  - Cover crops integrated with no/low till and late termination in NGP wheat rotations, which buffer inter-seed yield variability and reduce runoff/evaporation; when warm-season and late-terminated, they preserve soil water for subsequent wheat, producing measurable stability in the face of variable drought onset and intensity.<cite id="39250078-2">Warm-season covers may be safer due to lower water use; termination timing and species choice modulate moisture carryover.</cite> <cite id="39250078-1">Rainfall explained yield variability; termination did not significantly impact yield in that study period, indicating direct hydrologic and agronomic control over recovery.</cite>
- Supported primarily by proxies (limited direct drought-recovery measurement in NGP dryland cereals):
  - Pollinator counts for pulses/forages: While pollinators are critical for legume seed set and biodiversity, direct field evidence linking pollinator abundance to drought-year yield insurance in NGP small grains is weaker than direct hydrologic/management mechanisms; thus, pollinator counts function more as a conceptual proxy than a validated drought-recovery metric for these systems.<cite id="02e393cf-4">Field pea is an important pulse crop… diversified rotations enhanced biodiversity… but yield responses were tied to rainfall and N carryover rather than pollinator abundance.</cite>
  - Soil carbon accrual as a proxy for resilience: Replacing fallow with cover crops increased diversity and N but did not significantly change soil nitrate or soil organic matter over the study period; wheat yields tracked rainfall, indicating that short-term drought recovery is governed by hydrology and management rather than bulk SOC changes that typically accrue more slowly in semi-arid systems.<cite id="39250078-1">Termination treatments did not significantly impact soil nitrate or soil organic matter; rainfall explained yield variability.</cite> <cite id="02e393cf-4">Summer fallow retains water and N; wheat-fallow reduces soil organic matter and increases erosion, motivating diversification away from fallow.</cite>

Practical takeaways for the Northern Great Plains
- Prioritize rotation complexity that stores and partitions resources: Integrate warm-season pulse/forage phases and late-terminated covers to intercept summer storms, reduce runoff/evaporation, and leave moisture/N for the subsequent wheat; manage cereal–legume intercropping with relay timing and appropriate plant heights to reduce early competition and leverage deep-rooted/shallow-rooted complementarity under drought risk.<cite id="02e393cf-3">Practices that minimize runoff and evaporation will tend to maximize soil water storage during fallow periods… success depends on understanding rain events.</cite> <cite id="39250078-2">Warm-season covers may limit effects on subsequent wheat yields and be safer due to lower water use; termination timing and species choice matter.</cite> <cite id="f78bb409-1">Relay planting and basins conserve moisture and reduce competition under semi-arid rainfall regimes.</cite> <cite id="f78bb409-4">Complementary resource use raises yields by 20–67% vs monocultures, yet high legume density can suppress cereals.</cite>
- Use intercropping for risk-sharing across years: Nurse legumes can provide residual N and drought-tolerant layers that stabilize land productivity, but calibrate densities and spacing to avoid cereal suppression in dry springs; in years with adequate rainfall, intercropping maintains or increases total output while spreading drought risk across crops and seasons.<cite id="f78bb409-2">Residual N transfer can increase maize yield up to 66% after 2 years; cowpea fixes N and alters competition dynamics.</cite> <cite id="f78bb409-0">Despite component yield decreases, LER > 1.5 indicates higher land productivity in intercrops.</cite>
- Avoid proxy-only reliance in drought planning: In the NGP, plan for drought recovery through direct hydrologic and agronomic levers (species water-use phenology, residue management, and rainfall timing) rather than expecting soil carbon or pollinator abundance alone to buffer yield loss; validate site-specific with multi-year yield monitoring tied to rainfall/termination decisions.<cite id="39250078-1">In-season rainfall explained wheat yield variability; termination did not significantly impact yield in this study, underscoring agronomic/hydrologic control.</cite> <cite id="39250078-2">Warm-season cover crop choice and termination timing modulated moisture carryover and risk.</cite>
- Recognize trade-offs and uncertainty: Some diversification (e.g., early-fall cover mixes) can depress following wheat in dry years, while others (late-terminated warm-season covers, pulse inclusion) tend to be safer; intercropping can increase land productivity but may reduce component crop yields under high stress; more NGP-specific strip/relay intercropping trials under rainout or crusting disturbances would strengthen causal mechanisms linking biodiversity to recovery.<cite id="39250078-2">Maximum wheat reductions up to 60% after covers in dry years; warm-season covers safer due to lower water use.</cite> <cite id="f78bb409-4">Intercropping’s productivity gains rest on complementarity, but at high legume densities cereals can suffer in arid lands.</cite>

Summary
In the semi-arid Northern Great Plains, agrobiodiversity interventions with the strongest direct evidence for shock recovery are diversified rotations that replace fallow with pulses/forages and cover crops, and cereal–legume intercropping managed for complementarity and relay timing. These validate mechanisms of water interception and storage, N and moisture carryover, and competition management under actual rainfall variability and termination decisions. Proximal indicators like pollinator abundance and bulk soil carbon are better conceptual proxies than empirically validated drought-recovery metrics in these dryland cereals, where yields track rainfall and agronomic water-use phenology; thus, direct multi-year yield responses to rainfall and management should anchor decisions about crop rotation complexity and intercropping design in semi-arid systems.<cite id="02e393cf-3">Use of fallow and cover phases to store rainwater; practices that minimize runoff and evaporation increase storage.</cite> <cite id="02e393cf-4">Pulse inclusion increases wheat yields and reduces crop failure risk via N and moisture carryover.</cite> <cite id="39250078-1">In-season rainfall explains wheat yield variability better than cover biomass; termination did not significantly impact yield in that period.</cite> <cite id="f78bb409-2">Intercropping transfers residual N and improves land productivity; cowpea’s drought tolerance and N fixation underpin stability.</cite> <cite id="f78bb409-4">Complementary resource use raises yields but requires density/spacings that avoid cereal suppression under drought.</cite></answer>

Title: Long-Term Tillage on Yield and Water Use of Grain Sorghum and Winter Wheat
Snippet: been in place (Rusinamhodzi et al., 2011). Results of other studies have also suggested a crop, soil, and general location specifi c yield benefi t from NT compared with CT for sorghum, wheat, and other crops in the United States, specifi cally in the Great Plains region (Norwood et al., 1990;Norwood, 1992;Unger, 1994;Schlegel et al., 1999;Toliver et al., 2012;Farooq et al., 2011). 

Grain sorghum (Sorghum bicolor L.) and wheat are among the dominant dryland crops in the Great Plains region (USDA, 2016) and oft en grow in rotation between the two, as a wheatsorghum-fallow (WSF) system (Assefa et al., 2014;Hansen et al., 2012;Tarkalson et al., 2006). Even though both sorghum and wheat are adapted to dryland conditions, yield reduction in drought conditions is evident for both crops (Musick et al., 1994;Assefa and Staggenborg, 2010). Adoption of the appropriate tillage system contributes to mitigate the negative eff ects of water limitation. However, information on the eff ect of long-term tillage on wheat and sorghum grain yield, available soil water, and water productivity for a WSF system for the central Great Plains is limited. 

Th e objective of our study was to evaluate the eff ect of three long-term tillage intensities on wheat and sorghum yield, available soil water, and water productivity in a WSF rotation. Title: Introducing cover crops as a fallow replacement in the Northern Great Plains: I. Evaluation of cover crop mixes as a forage source for grazing cattle
Snippet: This research was part of a long-term study evaluating cover crops in a semi-arid region of the Northern Great Plains. Research was conducted at the Montana State University-Northern Agricultural Research Center near Havre, MT (48°29 ′ N, −109°48 ′ W) from 2012 to 2019. The research site is approximately 815 m above sea level, with an average annual precipitation of 305 mm. Soil is characterized as clay loam and classified as a Telstad-Joplin complex. The site is characterized as having 129 frost-free days and an average annual temperature of 5.94°C with an average high of 13.6°C and average low of 0.0°C. Weather data were collected onsite with official National Weather Service (NOAA) meteorological instruments. Recorded monthly mean, maximum and minimum temperatures and precipitation for April, May, June and July 2012 through 2019 and long-term averages  are presented in Table 1. 

This experiment was conducted as a randomized-completeblock design, where 29 individual species were utilized in 15 different cover crop mixtures in a wheat-cover crop rotation (Table 2). Cover crop mixtures were classified into three treatment groups, including (1) cool-season species, (2) warm-season species and (3) cool-and warm-season species mixture (mid-season). Both the commodity crop (spring and winter wheat) and each of the 15 cover crop mixtures were present in each of two adjacent fields (three replications per field) for each year of the study (2012)(2013)(2014)(2015)(2016)(2017)(2018)(2019). The cover crop mixtures were randomly allotted to plots (7.3 by 40.2 m) within each field the first year of the study and each treatment was planted in the same plot for the remainder of the trial in a wheat-cover crop rotation.

Title: Introducing cover crops as fallow replacement in the Northern Great Plains: II. Impact on following wheat crops
Snippet: The adoption of cover crops in replacement of fallow has been slow in the Northern Great Plains despite government incentives from American agencies. Reductions in wheat yields following cover crops were frequent enough and important enough to raise some concerns about their introduction in semi-arid cropping systems such as the Northern Great Plains. However, the previous year cover crop biomass was a poor predictor of wheat yields, whereas in-season rainfall explained more variability in wheat yields. Termination treatments did not significantly impact grain yield, soil nitrate or soil organic matter, which suggest the use of cover crops through grazing or hay could represent an economic benefit in this system. Further economic analyses are required to determine if the integration of livestock is necessary to mitigate the risks associated with the introduction of cover crops in replacement of fallow in the Northern Great Plains.

Title: Introducing cover crops as fallow replacement in the Northern Great Plains: II. Impact on following wheat crops
Snippet: Reductions in wheat yields following cover crops as a replacement of fallow were frequent enough and important enough to raise some concerns about their introduction in semi-arid cropping systems such as the Northern Great Plains. Maximum reductions were 1.4 t ha −1 (or a reduction of 60%) for winter wheat and 1.1 t ha −1 (35%) for spring wheat; such reductions are likely to have important consequences on the economic margin of production and it is, therefore, not surprising that agricultural producers in the semi-arid Northern Great Plains have been hesitant in their adoption of cover crops for conservation purposes. Similar concerns were raised more than 20 years ago by Unger and Vigil (1998) who suggested that cover crops were better suited to subhumid areas (>750 mm rainfall) compared to semi-arid areas. 

They further showed that greater conservation benefits were possible with no-till management, a practice that has been adopted widely in the region. What other management practices could be adopted in addition to no-till to improve soil conservation, and how much (or how soon) benefits could be expected remaining important questions. 

Our data also suggested that perhaps warm-season crops may limit the effect on subsequent wheat yields and be a safer alternative, possibly due to lower water use during the cover crop phase of the rotation. However, crop failures in these mixtures in 2012 and 2017, and the low biomass accumulation generally, demonstrated a poor performance as cover, let alone as forage (Wyffels et al., this issue). It is also doubtful that such low productivity and the lack of consistent cover would lead to the expected soil health benefits over the long term. This, however, is partially due to the delayed planting date compared to other mixtures and the early termination imposed in this study and might be addressed by growing these mixtures until the end of August or September, and used as forage during late summer or early fall to address a feeding gap in livestock operations during this period (Sedivec et al., 2015). How these mixtures may fit into the cropping systems of the Northern Great Plains also remains to be further investigated.

Title: Organic Agriculture and the Quest for the Holy Grail in Water-Limited Ecosystems: Managing Weeds and Reducing Tillage Intensity
Snippet: The Northern Great Plains (NGP) is a vast prairie landscape in South Dakota, North Dakota, and Montana; parts of Northeastern Wyoming and Northwestern Nebraska; the arable regions of the Canadian provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta; and Northeastern British Columbia [8]. Traditionally, agriculture in the NGP has been based on drought-resistant crops such as spring wheat (Triticum aestivum L.), and summer fallow is commonly used to conserve soil moisture and release organic nitrogen (N). More recently, the adoption of reduced tillage systems in conventionally managed systems has increased soil moisture retention and facilitated diversified rotations that include oilseed, pulse, forage, and other specialty crops [9,10]. These advances have made the NGP one of the largest U.S. expanses of conventional no-till dryland small grain, pulse, and oilseed agriculture [11]. This region also has great potential for small grain organic production [9] and for low-intensity organic sheep production, as animals are raised on dry native range and can be finished on cover crops integrated with crop production [12][13][14]. Despite its potential, the challenges of organic agriculture in dryland agroecosystems are many.

snippet.text: The adoption of cover crops in replacement of fallow has been slow in the Northern Great Plains despite government incentives from American agencies. Reductions in wheat yields following cover crops were frequent enough and important enough to raise some concerns about their introduction in semi-arid cropping systems such as the Northern Great Plains. However, the previous year cover crop biomass was a poor predictor of wheat yields, whereas in-season rainfall explained more variability in wheat yields. Termination treatments did not significantly impact grain yield, soil nitrate or soil organic matter, which suggest the use of cover crops through grazing or hay could represent an economic benefit in this system. Further economic analyses are required to determine if the integration of livestock is necessary to mitigate the risks associated with the introduction of cover crops in replacement of fallow in the Northern Great Plains.

snippet.text:
Reductions in wheat yields following cover crops as a replacement of fallow were frequent enough and important enough to raise some concerns about their introduction in semi-arid cropping systems such as the Northern Great Plains. Maximum reductions were 1.4 t ha −1 (or a reduction of 60%) for winter wheat and 1.1 t ha −1 (35%) for spring wheat; such reductions are likely to have important consequences on the economic margin of production and it is, therefore, not surprising that agricultural producers in the semi-arid Northern Great Plains have been hesitant in their adoption of cover crops for conservation purposes. Similar concerns were raised more than 20 years ago by Unger and Vigil (1998) who suggested that cover crops were better suited to subhumid areas (>750 mm rainfall) compared to semi-arid areas. 

They further showed that greater conservation benefits were possible with no-till management, a practice that has been adopted widely in the region. What other management practices could be adopted in addition to no-till to improve soil conservation, and how much (or how soon) benefits could be expected remaining important questions. 

Our data also suggested that perhaps warm-season crops may limit the effect on subsequent wheat yields and be a safer alternative, possibly due to lower water use during the cover crop phase of the rotation. However, crop failures in these mixtures in 2012 and 2017, and the low biomass accumulation generally, demonstrated a poor performance as cover, let alone as forage (Wyffels et al., this issue). It is also doubtful that such low productivity and the lack of consistent cover would lead to the expected soil health benefits over the long term. This, however, is partially due to the delayed planting date compared to other mixtures and the early termination imposed in this study and might be addressed by growing these mixtures until the end of August or September, and used as forage during late summer or early fall to address a feeding gap in livestock operations during this period (Sedivec et al., 2015). How these mixtures may fit into the cropping systems of the Northern Great Plains also remains to be further investigated.

The Northern Great Plains (NGP) is a vast prairie landscape in South Dakota, North Dakota, and Montana; parts of Northeastern Wyoming and Northwestern Nebraska; the arable regions of the Canadian provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta; and Northeastern British Columbia [8]. Traditionally, agriculture in the NGP has been based on drought-resistant crops such as spring wheat (Triticum aestivum L.), and summer fallow is commonly used to conserve soil moisture and release organic nitrogen (N). More recently, the adoption of reduced tillage systems in conventionally managed systems has increased soil moisture retention and facilitated diversified rotations that include oilseed, pulse, forage, and other specialty crops [9,10]. These advances have made the NGP one of the largest U.S. expanses of conventional no-till dryland small grain, pulse, and oilseed agriculture [11]. This region also has great potential for small grain organic production [9] and for low-intensity organic sheep production, as animals are raised on dry native range and can be finished on cover crops integrated with crop production [12][13][14]. Despite its potential, the challenges of organic agriculture in dryland agroecosystems are many. 

With a continental climate characterized by long, cold winters and short, warm summers, large diurnal ranges in temperature, strong winds, and variable and unpredictable precipitation [15], several environmental and biological factors hinder the sustainability of dryland organic agriculture across the NGP. First, in most years, soil moisture becomes depleted early in the summer and crops undergo terminal drought after anthesis, which reduces yield and impacts quality. This worrisome trend gets compounded as late winter/early spring temperatures have increased in the region since 1950 [16] and projections indicate that in areas within the NGP evapotranspiration constraints in mid-summer will increase [15], further increasing moisture challenges. It is predicted that the impacts of these new climate scenarios will become much more pronounced if temperatures rise above 31 • C and 35 • C during spring wheat anthesis and grain fill, respectively, or significant periods of unpredictable drought are experienced [17].

Title: Influence of height of maize variety on the productivity of intercropped maize ( Zea mays L.) and cowpea ( Vigna unguiculata (L.) Walp)
Snippet: A 2-year field study was conducted to compare the productivity of intercropped and monoculture maize and cowpea as influenced by the height of maize in the intercrop. During the 1994 and 1995 cropping seasons, IT 84E-124, a semi-erect, early-maturing, and photoperiod-insensitive cowpea cultivar, was planted with “Afo”, a short (1.2 m), early maturing, less vegetative, and AMRSR-Y, a tall (1.5 m), improved open-pollinated and of medium maturity group maize cultivars in a row intercropping. Yield components and grain yield of maize and cowpea were lower under intercropping than in monoculture systems. Intercropped cowpea yields were decreased by 29 and 26 per cent, respectively, under the short and tall maize varieties, while the yields of intercropped maize were reduced by 11 and 33 per cent for the short and tall varieties, respectively, across the two seasons. Land equivalent ration (LER) was, however, greater with the shorter maize variety than with the taller variety (1.60 vs 1.41), and was greater with the intercrops than with the monocultures (1.51 vs 1.00) across the two seasons. The results of this study indicate that although intercropping may result in decreases in the yield of one or both of the component crops in a maize-cowpea mixture, the productivity of a unit land area is higher with intercropping than with monoculture. The higher LER with the shorter maize variety in this study suggests that intercropping may be more remunerative when short and less vegetative cereal varieties are used in mixtures with legume crops. Title: Seasonal rainfall impacts the relative performance of maize-legume intercropping systems in semi-arid Zimbabwe
Snippet: The crops tested included a drought-tolerant maize variety (SC419), mucuna, and a landrace cowpea locally known as 'Nyadawa', suitable for grain and fodder due to high forage production. The cropping systems were: 

1. Sole maize 2. Sole cowpea 3. Sole mucuna 4. Maize-mucuna intercropping 5. Maize-cowpea intercropping Maize and mucuna were planted at an average depth of 5 cm in basins spaced at 90 cm between rows and 60 cm within rows, while sole cowpea was planted at 4-5 cm depth in basins at a spacing of 45 cm between rows and 30 cm within rows. Planting basins are recommended in semi-arid regions (receiving less than 600 mm seasonal rainfall) as they harvest rainfall and conserve soil  moisture. Maize and sole legumes were planted from 28 November and from 14 November during the 2021/22 and 2022/23 seasons, respectively. Depending on rainfall availability, the legume intercrops were relay planted 2-4 weeks after maize to reduce competition with maize (Masvaya et al., 2017). At planting, three or four seeds were dropped at each planting station and thinned down to two after crop emergence. For maize and mucuna, each station had two plants, resulting in a plant population density of 37,037 plants per hectare. Similarly, sole cowpea had two plants per station, resulting in a plant population density of 148,148 plants per hectare. Intercropped mucuna and cowpea were planted between the maize rows using hand hoes at 37,037 and 74,047 plants per hectare. Maize and mucuna seeds were obtained from local seed houses, namely Seed Co and Klein Karoo, respectively. Recommended fertiliser application rates were applied. Compound D fertilizer (7N:14P 2 O 5: 7K 2 O) was applied at a rate of 200 kg per hectare, providing 14 kg of nitrogen (N), 12.2 kg of phosphorus (P), and 11.6 kg of potassium (K) per hectare at planting in all treatments.

Title: ICT4Agroecology: a participatory research methodology for agroecological field research in Tanzania
Snippet: Legume intercropping -L.Cowpeas (Vigna unguiculata (L.) Walp.) are annual legumes, and they were chosen as they are widely used by local farmers and readily available, and are well-adapted to different agroecological zones in Tanzania (Matusso, Mugwe, and Mucheru-Muna 2014).The plant is well-adapted to heat and drought and can grow under low-fertility conditions (Ehlers and Hall 1997).Intercropping is defined as the "cultivation of two or more crops in the same space at the same time" (Matusso, Mugwe, and Mucheru-Muna 2014) and is advantageous in terms of nutrition, biodiversity, and productivity.These include risk minimization, support of a balanced nutrition, improved soil fertility, soil conservation, weed control, radiation use efficiency, and decreased spread of diseases or pests (Matusso, Mugwe, and Mucheru-Muna 2014).

Cultivation of cereals and legumes (such as cowpea) in the same space is practiced in Sub-Saharan Africa, especially in East Africa, where the combination of maize and cowpeas is common (Jensen et al. 2003).In addition to the aforementioned benefits of intercropping, combining maize and cowpeas has further advantages, such as the use of different nitrogen sources in the soil, which decreases the competition between both plants.Moreover, cowpea acts as a fertilizer due to its nitrogen-fixing capabilities.Residual nitrogen transfer in subsequent cropping cycles can increase maize yield up to 66% after 2 years of intercropping, in contrast to monocropping (Matusso, Mugwe, and Mucheru-Muna 2014).Furthermore, Jensen et al. (2003) obtained 7% higher maize yields in inter-cropped systems compared to mono-cropped maize, due to a direct nutrient transfer from the cowpea.However, the same study showed that under fertilized conditions, maize yield was lower in intercropped systems compared to mono-cropped systems.This might be due to greater competition between the crops resulting in higher cowpea yield.

Title: Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata (L.) Walp.) (Fabaceae) landrace diversity in Northern Ethiopia.
Snippet: As reported by Blade et al. (1997) and Timko et al. (2007), cowpea is usually grown as an intercrop with sorghum (Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench) and less frequently as a sole crop or intercropped with maize (Zea mays L.), cassava (Manihot esculenta Crantz), or cotton (Gossypium sp.).In the present study, cowpea is mainly grown as a rain fed crop and sorghum is the major cereal crop with which cowpea is intercropped (95%) in all surveyed areas, except in Werie Leke District where maize is the major cereal in which cowpea is intercropped (5%) along irrigation channels.Carlos (2004) and Dugje et al. (2009) described a similar intercropping system in West and Central Africa under similar semi-arid conditions, where cowpea was also intercropped with cereal crops (maize and sorghum) with the recommended spacing of 75 cm x 50 cm.Dugje et al. (2009) and AFF (2011) reported that fertilizer application in cowpea production depends on anticipated yield and soil fertility.As a legume, cowpea does not require much nitrogen because of the symbiotic nitrogen fixation.Based on the results, the majority of farmers (60%) indicated that they never used fertilizer and/or chemicals in the surveyed areas especially in Tanqua Abergelle, Abergelle, Sekota and Lasta Lalibela districts.On the other hand, reasonable number of the farmers (40%) used compost to improve soil fertility and chemical pesticides for plant protection in Bati, Kalu, Kola Temben and Werie Leke districts.

Title: Response of Intercropping Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor L. Moench) with Cowpea and Nitrogen Application on Growth and Yield of Sorghum
Snippet: Cereal-legume intercropping is a common practice in the tropics (Layek et al., 2018). The practice involves growing two or more crops on the same piece of land (Musa et al., 2012). Often, intercropping has advantages over sole cropping in terms of improved crop productivity, land sustainability, dietary diversity, and higher incomes (Sibhatu and Belete, 2015). For instance, an earlier study on cereal-legume intercropping found that the combined grain yield of cereal and legumes was higher by 20-67% compared with sole crops (Takele et al., 2017). This was attributed to the efficient utilization of water, radiation, and nutrients in crop mixtures (Liu et al., 2017). Nonetheless, intercropping has its limitations. For instance, a study on sorghum-cowpea intercropping in the arid and semi-arid lands (ASALs) in Ethiopia, reported a decrease in sorghum yield at higher cowpea density (Karanja et al., 2014). One of the essential tools to evaluate the productivity of intercropping systems, is the land equivalent ratio (LER), which expresses yields obtained in an intercrop system relative to the yield from a crop in a sole cropping system (Sibhatu and Belete, 2015). Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata (L.) Walp.) is a vital food legume in developing countries of the tropics and subtropics, particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa, Asia, and Central and South America. Its worldwide annual production is 3.5 million metric tons, and Nigeria only produced over 2.24 million metric tons on 2.52 million ha, followed by Niger, which produced 1.77 million metric tons on 5.57 million ha in 2016 (Chen et al., 2017). Cowpea is usually produced as a nutritious and highly edible food source. The seed nutritional description indicates that it contains 24% crude protein, 53% carbohydrates, and 2% fat. Because of cowpea is a excellent nutritional quality and value, it is referred to as the 'poor man's meat'.

snippet.text: Cereal-legume intercropping is a common practice in the tropics (Layek et al., 2018). The practice involves growing two or more crops on the same piece of land (Musa et al., 2012). Often, intercropping has advantages over sole cropping in terms of improved crop productivity, land sustainability, dietary diversity, and higher incomes (Sibhatu and Belete, 2015). For instance, an earlier study on cereal-legume intercropping found that the combined grain yield of cereal and legumes was higher by 20-67% compared with sole crops (Takele et al., 2017). This was attributed to the efficient utilization of water, radiation, and nutrients in crop mixtures (Liu et al., 2017). Nonetheless, intercropping has its limitations. For instance, a study on sorghum-cowpea intercropping in the arid and semi-arid lands (ASALs) in Ethiopia, reported a decrease in sorghum yield at higher cowpea density (Karanja et al., 2014). One of the essential tools to evaluate the productivity of intercropping systems, is the land equivalent ratio (LER), which expresses yields obtained in an intercrop system relative to the yield from a crop in a sole cropping system (Sibhatu and Belete, 2015). Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata (L.) Walp.) is a vital food legume in developing countries of the tropics and subtropics, particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa, Asia, and Central and South America. Its worldwide annual production is 3.5 million metric tons, and Nigeria only produced over 2.24 million metric tons on 2.52 million ha, followed by Niger, which produced 1.77 million metric tons on 5.57 million ha in 2016 (Chen et al., 2017). Cowpea is usually produced as a nutritious and highly edible food source. The seed nutritional description indicates that it contains 24% crude protein, 53% carbohydrates, and 2% fat. Because of cowpea is a excellent nutritional quality and value, it is referred to as the 'poor man's meat'.

A 2-year field study was conducted to compare the productivity of intercropped and monoculture maize and cowpea as influenced by the height of maize in the intercrop. During the 1994 and 1995 cropping seasons, IT 84E-124, a semi-erect, early-maturing, and photoperiod-insensitive cowpea cultivar, was planted with “Afo”, a short (1.2 m), early maturing, less vegetative, and AMRSR-Y, a tall (1.5 m), improved open-pollinated and of medium maturity group maize cultivars in a row intercropping. Yield components and grain yield of maize and cowpea were lower under intercropping than in monoculture systems. Intercropped cowpea yields were decreased by 29 and 26 per cent, respectively, under the short and tall maize varieties, while the yields of intercropped maize were reduced by 11 and 33 per cent for the short and tall varieties, respectively, across the two seasons. Land equivalent ration (LER) was, however, greater with the shorter maize variety than with the taller variety (1.60 vs 1.41), and was greater with the intercrops than with the monocultures (1.51 vs 1.00) across the two seasons. The results of this study indicate that although intercropping may result in decreases in the yield of one or both of the component crops in a maize-cowpea mixture, the productivity of a unit land area is higher with intercropping than with monoculture. The higher LER with the shorter maize variety in this study suggests that intercropping may be more remunerative when short and less vegetative cereal varieties are used in mixtures with legume crops. Summary and framing
In semi-arid Northern Great Plains (NGP) cropping systems, agrobiodiversity interventions that stabilize yields in the short term—via pollinator support (floral strips, forage/seed mixes, mass-flowering crops) or annual pest regulation (habitat diversification, intercropping, cover crops that recruit natural enemies)—can conflict with long-term soil carbon (C) accumulation when they increase aboveground or rhizosphere C losses, favor C4 pathways with higher respiratory losses, or export biomass outside the field system. The direction and magnitude of soil C change depend on the balance of C inputs (residue and root inputs, rhizodeposits) and C losses (soil respiration, denigration/oxidation, export via grazing/harvest, and off-site transport). Evidence from NGP rotations, prairie/flower strips, and cover crop trials shows that some pollinator- and pest-support strategies boost biodiversity and ecosystem services with modest or early soil C gains, while others can reduce SOC or impose management costs that undermine long-term C storage. <cite id="f45b9a9e-2">Prairie strips increased soil organic carbon and biodiversity while maintaining yields in early years</cite><cite id="58f54fad-2">Mass-flowering legumes provide temporary floral resources and can reduce fertilizer needs but still sequester soil C at moderate rates in their early years</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-0">Leguminous pulses in rotation can reduce cumulative CO2 efflux and SOC sequestration relative to cereals, whereas continuous spring wheat or pea–wheat rotations sometimes accrue higher SOC</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-3">Flower strips that maximize plant diversity tend to be less productive and still add substantial C to soil, with permanent strips acting as significant C sinks</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-3">In NGP, grazing/hay termination of cover crops often showed no significant change in SOC in the second year</cite>.

Pollinator-support interventions: when short-term stability conflicts with long-term SOC
- Mechanisms of short-term stability: sequential and mass-flowering crops, floral strips, and hedgerows increase spatio-temporal continuity and abundance of pollinators, boosting pollination services and biocontrol spillover into cropland; these effects are robust across semi-arid and temperate contexts. <cite id="58f54fad-4">Increasing landscape complexity via intercropping, cover crops, and crop-livestock mixtures increases floral resources and habitat for pollinators and stabilizes pollinator communities</cite><cite id="58f54fad-2">Annual flowering fields (mass-flowering legumes/beans) raise pollinator abundance and species richness, and can fix N, but still deliver C sequestration via residue inputs to soil</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-0">Prairie strips concentrated litter inputs near edges and showed subtle but detectable increases in “active carbon” adjacent to strips in the first post-mowing year</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-1">Prairie strips and reduced land-use intensity increased pollination, butterflies, spiders, and dung beetles with clear spillover gradients</cite>.
- Conflicts with long-term SOC:
  1) Biomass removal and export: when floral/forage strips are harvested for seed or silage, or when cover crops are taken as hay/forage, added C is removed from the system, lowering net SOC accumulation. <cite id="f45b9a9e-3">Flower strips not harvested have much greater C input to soil than croplands; areas with high external organic C inputs (manure/biomass) show lower incremental C sequestration, and only permanent strips act as significant C sinks</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-3">Termination by grazing or hay showed no significant change in SOC in the second year, suggesting that when biomass is removed, C gains are offset and require economic integration to be viable</cite>. In semi-arid rotations, legumes like lentils and chickpeas produce less straw C than wheat and can reduce cumulative CO2 efflux and SOC accrual compared to cereals, highlighting that “temporary” floral pulses may add pollinator services but reduce residue-driven SOC inputs. <cite id="b31e37fd-0">Straw C was 26–74% lower for pulses than spring wheat; root biomass and rhizodeposits were 24–31% lower for pulse–wheat than wheat–wheat; SOC sequestration rate was greater for pea and spring wheat than chickpea/lentil, or greater for pea–wheat than other rotations</cite>.
  2) High-diversity, low-biomass strips: maximizing plant species richness reduces total biomass production, which can lower direct C inputs even as it supports pollinator richness. <cite id="f45b9a9e-3">A significant negative correlation between unique plant species and total biomass in flower strips indicates that highly diverse strips are less productive, yet still have greater C input than cropland; there is a trade-off between maximizing biodiversity and C sequestration in flower strips</cite>.
  3) C4 pulse dominance and respiratory losses: pulses (C4) often have higher photosynthetic rates but greater respiratory CO2 efflux; in rotations, this can reduce net C storage relative to C3 cereals when pulses replace cereals in cereal phases. <cite id="b31e37fd-0">Cumulative CO2 flux from May to April was 14–17% greater for continuous spring wheat than pulse–wheat rotations; SOC sequestration rates are higher for pea and spring wheat than chickpea and lentil</cite>. In NGP rotations, soybean and lentil improved subsequent wheat yields and protein, yet the cereal phase’s replacement by legumes reduced net C inputs and SOC gains compared to wheat-only rotations. <cite id="b31e37fd-1">Soybean and lentil grown immediately before wheat enhanced yields and protein; however, rotation dynamics showed cereal phases benefit ecological processes, and leguminous stubbles altered growth trajectories</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-0">Pulse–wheat rotations had 5–16% lower carbon balance than wheat–wheat, indicating greater C loss or lower net sequestration</cite>.
  4) Off-site export and wind/ice damage: tall, dense floral/forage strips and grassed waterways can increase litter and herbivory pressure and create disservices like herbivory drag; if biomass is periodically mowed or grazed and exported, net C inputs decline. <cite id="f45b9a9e-0">Prairie strips increased active carbon near edges; mowing in 2019 caused a spillover of prairie litter inputs into cropland, highlighting biogeochemical benefits and potential disservices like herbivory that were not measured</cite>.
- Management choices that create the tradeoff:
  - Annual mass-flowering forage crops (e.g., clovers, peas) used as seed/forage: deliver short-term pollinator stability and N fixation but, when harvested, remove C that would otherwise accrue in soil; risk higher in arid years when inputs are limited and residues are small. <cite id="58f54fad-2">Legumes provide ample temporary food resources for pollinators and reduce fertilizer demand; their C inputs contribute to soil C accrual when left in place</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-3">Only permanent flower strips act as significant C sinks; high external inputs reduce incremental C gains</cite>.
  - High-diversity wildflower strips sown as temporary habitat: enhance pollinator richness and stability but often reduce total biomass; net C addition to soil exists, yet the per-area C sequestration rate can be lower than lower-diversity, higher-biomass strips. <cite id="f45b9a9e-3">More species correlate with less total biomass, with modeled C sequestration ~0.48 Mg C ha−1 year−1 in early years; trade-off between biodiversity and C accrual</cite>.
  - Pulses replacing cereal phases in rotations: improve yield stability and protein but reduce SOC sequestration relative to cereals due to lower straw/root C and higher respiratory losses; in NGP, this can appear as improved agronomic stability without commensurate long-term C gain. <cite id="b31e37fd-0">Pulse–wheat rotations had lower SOC sequestration rates than wheat–wheat; continuous wheat or pea–wheat sometimes accrue more SOC</cite>.
  - Livestock integration with cover/forage strips: grazing can convert C inputs to animal products with local feed value; hay/seed removal likewise departs the system. When properly integrated, these systems can maintain or improve SOC due to persistent litter and reduced tillage, but when biomass is repeatedly exported, SOC gains are limited. <cite id="b31e37fd-3">Termination by grazing or hay did not significantly change SOC in the second year but suggested economic benefits via forage, implying that livestock integration can mitigate risks of replacing fallow</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-4">Prairie strips reduce erosion and support biodiversity; cover crops and reduced tillage generally increase biodiversity and nutrient availability, whereas tillage and pesticides decrease biodiversity and increase GHG emissions</cite>.

Pest-regulation interventions: when short-term stability conflicts with long-term SOC
- Mechanisms of short-term stability: habitat diversification (hedgerows, field borders, intercropping), cover crops, and crop-livestock mixtures recruit and sustain natural enemies and reduce pest outbreaks; these practices increase floral and nesting resources and habitat connectivity, stabilizing yields via biocontrol. <cite id="58f54fad-4">Increasing habitat complexity and connectivity through hedgerows, cover crops, and polyculture systems promotes wild pollinator diversity and stability</cite><cite id="58f54fad-1">Floral resource diversity and abundance in diversified horticultural systems support comparable pollinator richness and abundance to semi-natural grasslands, complementing specialized habitats</cite>.
- Conflicts with long-term SOC:
  1) Increased standing biomass and herbivory: diversified pest-regulation habitats often increase aboveground productivity and insect community complexity, which can elevate herbivory and disease pressure; when these pressures are managed with herbicides or fungicides, input-induced C emissions offset soil C gains. <cite id="58f54fad-0">Diversification improves heterogeneity and connectivity for pollinators but requires long-term study on crops to diversify with and how landscape context modulates effects</cite><cite id="58f54fad-3">Land-use changes alter pollinator communities with consequences for plant fitness; mass flowering crops can mediate pollinator spatial distribution, affecting plant–pollinator and plant–herbivore dynamics</cite>. In semi-arid NGP, cover crops terminated by grazing/hay showed no immediate SOC change; persistent biomass and increased pest pressure can drive growers toward inputs that raise net C losses. <cite id="b31e37fd-3">Cover crops as fallow replacement often showed no significant change in SOC in the second year, with termination method not significantly impacting SOC, underscoring the need for economic/livestock integration to mitigate risk</cite>.
  2) Carbon losses via denigration/oxidation of fine roots and rhizodeposits under stress: diversified systems with high root exudation can increase microbial activity; under semi-arid stress, pulses (C4) and certain intercropping combinations elevate respiratory CO2, reducing net C storage despite increased belowground inputs. <cite id="b31e37fd-0">Root biomass and rhizodeposits were 24–31% greater for wheat–wheat than pulse–wheat, yet cumulative CO2 flux was 14–17% greater in continuous wheat; SOC sequestration rates favored cereals over C4 pulses</cite>.
  3) Timing and precipitation variability: in semi-arid systems, pest-regulation benefits are highly weather-dependent. Intercrops and cover crops may suppress early-season pests but can also compete with the cash crop, lowering first-year yields; when moisture is poor, termination by grazing/hay diverts C away from soil, and any SOC gains are delayed or negated. <cite id="b31e37fd-1">Canola stubble did not offer immediate wheat yield advantages but supported high and stable yields in subsequent years; monoculture cereal rotations were more detrimental to hard red spring wheat than to winter wheat, highlighting crop- and phase-specific tradeoffs</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-2">At a 305 mm precipitation site in Montana, alternating wheat with cover crop mixtures (radish, lentil, pea, oat, turnip, sorghum-sudangrass, soybean) was practiced to protect soil moisture; this context underscores how functional groups are adopted to deliver multiple services</cite>.
- Management choices that create the tradeoff:
  - Annual intercropping with pest-suppressive legumes (e.g., soybean–wheat) for insurance: improves early-season pest regulation and nutrient complementarity but can reduce SOC inputs compared to cereal intercrops and increase risk of herbivory and disease requiring inputs. <cite id="b31e37fd-1">Soybean and lentil immediately prior to wheat enhanced yields and protein; their stubbles supported superior in-season growth, illustrating ecological benefits alongside potential for increased pest pressure</cite>.
  - Herbaceous borders and wildflower strips adjacent to cash crops: increase natural enemy diversity and pollination services but can increase herbivory disservices; if managed with frequent herbicide applications to suppress weeds and pests, net C sink potential declines. <cite id="58f54fad-0">Outstanding questions include which crops to diversify with and how farming intensity modulates effects on pollinators</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-0">Prairie strips spillover benefits included active carbon near edges; potential ecosystem disservices like herbivory were noted and warrant study</cite>.
  - Cover crops sown as forage/hay in semi-arid rotations: deliver short-term soil protection and moisture retention but often show no immediate SOC change when terminated; if biomass is exported, net SOC can decline. Economic integration with grazing reduces this export and can maintain SOC via persistent litter and reduced tillage. <cite id="b31e37fd-3">Termination treatments did not significantly impact SOC in the second year, suggesting cover crops can be integrated as forage to add economic value while preserving or improving SOC with proper management</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-4">Cover crops and reduced till generally increase biodiversity and nutrient availability, whereas tillage and pesticides decrease biodiversity and increase GHG emissions</cite>.

When and where the conflict arises in NGP practice
- Early vs. late season and multi-year dynamics: Pollinator-support via prairie/flower strips accrues measurable SOC near edges within 1–3 years in NGP-like semi-arid settings, especially under lower land-use intensity; however, first-year mowing or biomass export reverses this by removing litter inputs, creating a short-term stability (forage/seed) vs. long-term SOC tradeoff. <cite id="f45b9a9e-2">Soil organic carbon and multiple biodiversity metrics increased with reduced land use intensity; benefits spilled over within 1–3 years</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-0">Mowing strips in 2019 caused a spillover of prairie litter into cropland in adjacent sites, highlighting that management timing and disturbance alter C inputs</cite>.
- Crop identity and phase: Replacing cereal phases with legumes (e.g., lentil–wheat or continuous legumes) improves agronomic stability via N fixation and diverse blooms but reduces net SOC compared to cereals due to lower straw/root C and higher respiration; conversely, continuous cereals or pea–wheat rotations often accrue higher SOC, creating a tradeoff between pest-suppressive legumes and long-term C storage. <cite id="b31e37fd-0">Pulse–wheat rotations had 5–16% lower carbon balance than wheat–wheat; root biomass and rhizodeposits were lower in pulses; SOC sequestration favored cereals</cite>.
- Intensification and inputs: Pest-regulation through diversified habitats can spur herbivory and disease, pushing farmers toward inputs (herbicides/fungicides) that increase net GHGs and erode SOC benefits; this is particularly acute in semi-arid years when moisture stress reduces cereal competitiveness and prompts more intensive management. <cite id="58f54fad-0">Designing long-term studies on how crop diversification benefits wild pollinators remains essential; farming intensity and landscape context modulate effects</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-3">Second-year SOC showed no significant change with cover crops, emphasizing the need for economic/livestock integration to mitigate risks</cite>.
- Spatial configuration and permanence: Temporary, high-diversity floral strips add C but at lower per-area rates; permanent native prairie strips and native perennial borders act as stronger C sinks and stabilize multiple services, reducing conflict by embedding C in long-lived soil pools. <cite id="f45b9a9e-3">Flower strips not harvested add substantial C to soil; only permanent strips act as significant C sinks; more species correlate with less biomass and modeled C sequestration</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-2">Prairie strips increased SOC and biodiversity with reduced land use intensity, with benefits spilling over into cropland</cite>.

Management levers to align short-term stability with long-term SOC in NGP
- Prefer native prairie strips and perennial borders over annual wildflower seed mixes where feasible: native, perennial systems build SOC faster and provide persistent habitat, reducing biomass export and herbivory drag; integrate livestock grazing to recycle nutrients in situ rather than removing hay/seed. <cite id="f45b9a9e-2">Prairie strips increased SOC and ecosystem services early in establishment and with reduced land-use intensity</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-3">Permanent flower strips are significant C sinks; high external inputs reduce incremental gains</cite>.
- Use cereal-dominant rotations with targeted floral intercrops or late-season “green manure” phases: cereal phases increase residue C and SOC accrual; insert legumes or brassicas as short-duration pest-regulation or pollinator-support phases only when moisture supports them, then terminate and graze to keep C local. <cite id="b31e37fd-0">Wheat–wheat or pea–wheat rotations accrue higher SOC than pulse–wheat; SOC sequestration is greater for cereals</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-1">Legumes immediately prior to wheat enhanced yields and protein; cereal phases can leverage ecological benefits while maintaining residue inputs</cite>.
- Design floral and habitat strips for high C retention: favor lower-diversity, higher-biomass mixes or shorter-duration sow–terminate–graze rotations; place strips on wind-exposed edges to reduce aboveground loss, and avoid mowing unless needed for weed control. <cite id="f45b9a9e-3">More species correlate with less biomass and a trade-off between biodiversity and C sequestration; modeled C accrual ~0.48 Mg C ha−1 year−1 early years</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-0">Mowing prairie strips altered litter spillover and active carbon near edges, underscoring management timing effects</cite>.
- Tighten pest-regulation design to minimize herbivory: select intercrops and borders with complementary phenology and pest repulsion, maintain competitive cereals in dry years, and use thresholds-based IPM to avoid blanket herbicide that erodes SOC. <cite id="b31e37fd-2">Cover crop mixes in NGP were selected for multiple ecosystem services, reflecting functional group complementarity under water-limited conditions</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-1">Monoculture cereal rotations were more detrimental to hard red spring wheat than to winter wheat, emphasizing crop-specific ecological tradeoffs</cite>.
- Weather- and phase-tailor habitat strategies: in canola-dominant rotations, retain stubble and delay termination to preserve residue C; in legume-heavy phases, compensate for lower SOC by boosting cereal follow-on crops and using reduced till to maximize residue retention. <cite id="b31e37fd-1">Canola stubble supported high and stable yields in subsequent wheat and HRSW when planted; monoculture cereal rotations were more detrimental to HRSW than WW</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-4">Reduced tillage generally increases biodiversity and nutrient availability; tillage and pesticides increase GHG emissions</cite>.
- Recognize the role of plant metabolism: avoid long-term dominance by C4 legumes where SOC accrual is the goal; sequence C4 pulses to pest-prone early spring windows, then terminate and reincorporate into cereal phases that favor SOC. <cite id="b31e37fd-0">Pulses have higher cumulative CO2 efflux and lower SOC sequestration rates than cereals; continuous wheat or pea–wheat often outpace pulses in SOC accrual</cite>.

Practical takeaways for NGP farmers and advisors
- Conflict windows: The clearest conflicts occur when pollinator- or pest-support biomass is harvested (seed/forage/hay), when legumes replace cereal phases for extended periods, or when diversified habitats trigger herbicide/fungicide escalation. <cite id="f45b9a9e-3">Biomass removal reduces incremental SOC; only permanent habitat acts as a strong C sink</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-0">Pulse–wheat rotations had lower SOC sequestration than wheat–wheat</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-3">Second-year SOC effects of cover crops were minimal when terminated by grazing/hay, indicating potential for economic integration to maintain SOC</cite>.
- Win–win windows: Early establishment of native prairie strips and native perennial borders under reduced tillage; cereal–cover crop rotations with on-farm grazing; and polyculture sequences that ensure floral continuity without biomass export. <cite id="f45b9a9e-2">Prairie strips increased SOC and biodiversity under reduced land-use intensity with early benefits</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-4">Cover crops and reduced tillage increase biodiversity and nutrient cycling while limiting GHGs</cite>.
- Measurement and planning: Quantify enterprise-level gains from pollination/pest control and livestock forage against SOC accrual goals; sequence rotations to use high-SOC cereal phases as anchors, and deploy legumes/flower strips strategically. <cite id="b31e37fd-1">Adopting winter wheat into cereal phases can accrue synergistic ecological benefits with multiple rotational crops</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-0">Rotation choice measurably shifts C balance and SOC sequestration rates</cite>.

Bottom line
In semi-arid NGP cropping, pollinator-support and annual pest-regulation interventions that deliver short-term stability often conflict with long-term soil C accumulation when they export biomass, favor C4 pulses with higher respiratory losses, or trigger input-intensive management; the tradeoff is strongest for annual forage/seed floral strips, high-diversity low-biomass mixes, and legume-heavy rotations. Aligning goals requires permanent native habitat, cereal-dominant SOC phases, targeted floral and pest-regulation strips sited for C retention, and livestock integration to keep biomass cycling on-farm. <cite id="f45b9a9e-3">Flower strips add C when left permanent and unharvested, with modeled early-year sequestration comparable to cover crops and grassland conversion</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-0">Cereal-based rotations and pea–wheat generally accrue higher SOC than pulse–wheat due to greater residue inputs and lower efflux</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-3">When cover crops are grazed or harvested for hay, SOC changes are minimal in the short term, but economic and management integration are needed to avoid net C loss</cite>.

Title: Crop diversification for pollinator conservation
Snippet: Crop diversification has gained momentum because of the many benefits it can have for farmers and the environment (Tamburini et al. 2020;Beillouin et al. 2021;Nicholson and Williams 2021). Crop fields are not as stable and diverse as natural habitats, and cannot replace the importance of semi-natural habitat for pollinator conservation (Batáry et al. 2015;Eeraerts 2023;Fijen et al. 2024), we highlight the potential of crop diversification practices as an additional pollinator conservation measure (Table 1; Fig. 2). Crop diversification can enhance spatio-temporal flower resource availability, continuity and accessibility without too drastic adjustments for farmers, while also improving the landscape heterogeneity and functional connectivity for pollinators. With large changes ahead in the agricultural system driven by climate change and the need for a more plant-based diet, it is essential to design long-term studies on how crop diversification can benefit wild pollinators. Outstanding questions include what crops to diversify with, and how landscape context and farming intensity can modulate the effect on crop diversification practices on wild pollinators. Combined effects of multiple crop diversification practices on wild pollinators are also virtually unknown. Crop diversification with both agricultural production and pollinator conservation in mind can provide synergies without taking a substantial part of land out of production: after all, farmers need pollinators for high yields of many crops (Turo et al. 2024)
</snippet>
