Title: Small-scale, diverse horticultural systems and semi-natural grasslands support complementary pollinator populations
Snippet: Pollinating insects are of great importance in natural ecosystems and agricultural landscapes. Despite their crucial role for food production, safeguarding pollination services is becoming increasingly challenging due to pollinator declines. Habitat loss and agricultural intensification are among the main drivers, causing a substantial reduction in the availability of floral resources. Despite efforts, the uptake of measures to halt these declines in agricultural landscapes is low. Implementation of a novel crop production system is therefore proposed as a solution to ensure food security whilst concomitantly minimising environmental degradation and the associated biodiversity loss. Agricultural diversification is one such strategy that is known to promote multiple ecosystem services. Yet, the effects of agricultural diversification on pollinator populations in farm-scale, observational studies remains understudied. Here, we examine the importance of small-scale, diverse horticultural systems (SDHS) to support wild pollinator communities. Floral resources and wild pollinators were sampled in both SDHSs and semi-natural grasslands (SNG) in 16 landscapes in Flanders, Belgium. During late summer, these SNGs provide and important source of floral resources, thereby serving as a benchmark habitat to which the SDHSs are compared. Our study highlights the value of SDHSs as they provide diverse and abundant floral resources compared to SNGs. Moreover, pollinator species richness and abundance were comparable between the two habitats. Conversely, floral resource and pollinator community composition differed, indicating that different pollinator communities used the complementary resources provided by both habitat types. Furthermore, we show that SNGs represent the most specialised habitat type. We therefore argue that SDHSs can be considered to be an additional, complementary source of floral resources to those provided by SNGs. However, these SDHSs cannot substitute SNGs, given the importance of these grasslands for pollinators.
</snippet>
<snippet id=58f54fad-2>
Title: No evidence of decline in bumblebee abundance and species richness from edge to interior in moderately-sized red clover fields
Snippet: Agricultural intensification and associated changes in land use have substantially decreased local biodiversity (Ramankutty et al. 2008;Jaureguiberry et al. 2022). Such declines in biodiversity directly influence a wide range of ecosystem functions, ultimately impacting both the remaining natural habitats as well as agricultural fields. For instance, intensified agriculture reduces resources available to pollinators, leading to lower pollinator abundance and species richness within agricultural landscapes (Potts et al. 2010;Dupont et al. 2011;Goulson et al. 2015). In turn, the decrease in pollinator populations can lead to insufficient pollination, ultimately reducing crop yields (Garibaldi et al. 2009;Jing et al. 2021). 

To persist in agricultural landscapes, wild pollinators need appropriate nesting and foraging sites, which are scarce in intensively managed fields. Enhancing habitat diversity within agricultural areas has been suggested as a way to mitigate this limitation and improve pollination services provided by wild pollinators (e.g., Potts et al. 2016;Garibaldi et al. 2021). Such diversification measures include floral enhancements along field margins (e.g., hedgerows or wildflower plantings), adding natural habitat features at the landscape level (e.g., increasing the proportion of natural vegetation cover), and cultivating massflowering crops that provide forage for pollinators. 

One of the most widely adopted practices to mitigate the effects of intensive agriculture and support wild pollinators is the cultivation of annual flowering fields. In the European Union, this measure is included in the mandatory agri-environmental schemes under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP). Under these schemes, farmers are subsidized for managing their land for the benefit of natural habitats and species, including through intercropping. The mass-flowering crops cultivated in these annual flowering fields include legumes, such as clovers and beans. Legumes provide ample, albeit temporary, food resources for many pollinating insects, thereby increasing their abundance and species richness in agroecosystems. Additionally, they enhance soil fertility through nitrogen fixation, reducing the need for synthetic fertilizers, and they can be harvested for seeds and silage.
</snippet>
<snippet id=58f54fad-3>
Title: Human-Mediated Land Use Change Drives Intraspecific Plant Trait Variation
Snippet: Because many pollinators utilize both wild plants and crops, sharing local pollinators creates potential fitness implications through interference in visitation rates or pollen transfer (Stanley and Stout, 2014). For example, mass blooming crops can mediate the spatial distribution of pollinators in the landscape, reducing visitation and fitness in coblooming wild plants (Holzschuh et al., 2011;Van Reeth et al., 2019). Conversely, mass crop blooms may augment pollinator populations, increasing spillover and boosting the fitness of wild plants blooming immediately after the crop (Kovács-Hostyánszki et al., 2013). Therefore, mass flowering crops can have opposing outcomes for wild plant populations via separate mechanisms suggesting that the kind of habitat conversion as well as the traits of focal wild plant populations are likely to have strong impacts on the outcome of these land use changes on wild plant populations. 

In some systems, plants demonstrate resilience to land use change. This is exemplified when there is no detectable effect of land use change on plant reproductive success (Lopes and Buzato, 2007;Ekroos et al., 2015;Skogen et al., 2016;Grass et al., 2018) likely because these landscapes select for pollinator species that are tolerant to disturbance and/or have a high dispersal ability. In restored prairies, increasing proportion of agriculture in the surrounding landscape did not increase pollen limitation in a pollinator dependent forb (Ritchie et al., 2020). It is possible that the restored prairies provide habitat to support sufficient pollinators to prevent pollen limitation. Further, conflicting pressures of pollinators and herbivores could also be responsible for the failure of these studies to detect a fitness effect of landscape composition (Steffan-Dewenter et al., 2001). 

In summary, land use changes have substantial impacts on the composition of pollinator communities with potential consequences on plant fitness in remaining natural habitat fragments. As a rule, loss of natural habitat is expected to reduce the abundance and diversity of wild plant pollinators and consequently cause pollen limitation in wild plants (Taki et al., 2007); yet, exceptions to this rule, such as temporal effects of mass flowering crops, will alter these dynamics.
</snippet>

Snippet: For example, Sardiñas et al. (2016) found that groundnesting native bees nested both within fields and edges, and that due to short actual foraging distances, visitation by bees nesting in and around fields led to a patchy distribution of pollination services across the field. 

Taking this knowledge into consideration, and within the ecological intensification framework (Table 1), restored or maintained semi-natural ecosystems, field border plantings and riparian buffer strips, can directly increase the complexity and connectivity of agricultural landscapes, often improving floral and nesting resources for pollinator diversity (Lagerl€ of et al. 1992;Carvell et al. 2004;Cole et al. 2015;Kremen & M'Gonigle 2015;Baude et al. 2016;Ponisio et al. 2016). Optimising management of these semi-natural areas, such as by adjusting mowing frequency and rotation, can diversify flower and insect pollinator communities (Noordijk et al. 2009;Halbritter et al. 2015) across the landscape. 

Increasing landscape complexity by employing crop and crop-livestock mixtures, intercropping and cover crops can increase floral resources and habitat for many pollinator species, even in landscapes with little semi-natural land-cover types (Williams & Kremen 2007;Bat ary et al. 2011;Kennedy et al. 2013). Increasing connectivity by reducing distances between foraging resources elevates pollinator diversity and abundance in fields (Ricketts et al. 2008;Kennedy et al. 2013;Clough et al. 2014). Diversified agricultural systems typified by a large number of crop types and small field sizes (Fahrig et al. 2015) promote wild pollinator diversity, community stability and pollination success of crops and wild plants ( Kremen & Miles 2012;Kennedy et al. 2013). Polyculture systems with sequentially flowering or co-flowering crops assure efficient pollination of plants differing in flower phenology by providing seasonal and spatial continuity of food resources supporting pollinator diversity and abundance (Mayfield & Belavadi 2008;Rundl€ of et al. 2014;Ponisio et al. 2015).

Title: Prairie Strips and Lower Land Use Intensity Increase Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
Snippet: We were surprised that prairie strips increased pollination as our plot sizes are a fraction of pollinator foraging range (Ricketts et al., 2008), and we suspect that pollinators were attracted to the high concentration of resources that contrasted strongly with crops. For active carbon, the effect of distance from prairie strip may have been driven by high prairie litter inputs. Mowing prairie strips in 2019 may have caused a spillover of prairie litter inputs into cropland that did not occur in 2020, leading to higher levels of active carbon in crop soils immediately adjacent to prairie strips. While the increase of active carbon in nearby sites was subtle, it still highlights the biogeochemical benefits of adjacent prairies for agricultural lands, which are generally underappreciated (Pérez-Suárez et al., 2014). 

Our study shows that spillover effects from prairie strips extend across measures of biodiversity and ecosystem services. Pollinators and pollination services have been studied at distances from restorations and habitat edges, often with higher numbers of pollinators and rates of pollination near non-crop habitat (Ricketts, 2004;Carvalheiro et al., 2010;Kordbacheh et al., 2020); by also demonstrating this phenomenon in dung beetles, spiders, active carbon, and decomposition, we show that these spatial effects apply to a broader array of organisms and ecosystem services. These results, with detailed attention to mechanism in our controlled experiment, strengthen evidence that suggests that strategic placement and amount of natural habitat in agricultural landscapes can add both conservation value and ecosystem services to an agricultural landscape (Basso et al., 2019;Mitchell et al., 2021). Our study focused on ecosystem services, and we did not measure potential ecosystem disservices from prairie strips that could impact yield, such as herbivory, however, such disservices could be addressed in future studies. 

Prairie strips require several years after planting to resemble a restored prairie community, over which time diversity and ecosystem services have been shown to accrue (Kurtz, 2013;Griffin et al., 2017). Supporting this, we found that year since prairie strip establishment affected all responses that we measured at distances from prairie strips except ant richness (Figure 4).

Title: Prairie Strips and Lower Land Use Intensity Increase Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
Snippet: We show that prairie strips, even early in their establishment, combined with lower land use intensity can promote biodiversity and ecosystem services without compromising crop yield. Within reduced input and biologically based treatments, where sampling effort occurred within prairie strips and at increasing distance from strips, biodiversity and ecosystem services spilled over into agronomic areas for five out of six measures. Among all treatments, using data from the entire plot area (not sampling within prairie strips for treatments with strips), pollination services and the abundance of butterflies and spiders were higher in plots with prairie strips. In addition, soil organic carbon, butterfly richness, and spider richness increased with a decrease in land use intensity. Crop yield in the reduced input treatment was equal to that of conventional management, even while including the area taken out of production. These effects were evident early in strip establishment, during which prairie strip plant communities changed from mostly weeds to a diversity of planted species. We expect the effects of strips to grow over time as native plants establish and become more abundant, and as lagged effects of historic agronomic disturbances abate. 

The benefits of prairie strips decreased with distance into cropland for spider abundance and richness, dung beetle abundance, active carbon, decomposition, and pollination (Figure 4). Each of these responses decreased with distance from the prairie strip, but did so by different mechanisms. For spiders, the spillover into cropland was delayed one year after the prairie strips were sown. Prairie strips provided new habitat and sources of prey for spiders (Hussain et al., 2021), such that spiders could move into cropland to capture additional prey. The impact on dung beetles and decomposition are likely due to the prairie strips harboring dung beetles in the year after restoration, which in turn caused a higher rate of manure removal near the prairie strips and a decrease in dung beetle abundance and manure removal with increasing distance from the strips (Manning and Cutler, 2018). For pollination, prairie strips increased floral resources which attracted pollinators and then exported them into the surrounding habitat (Garibaldi et al., 2011). We were surprised that prairie strips increased pollination as our plot sizes are a fraction of pollinator foraging range (Ricketts et al., 2008), and we suspect that pollinators were attracted to the high concentration of resources that contrasted strongly with crops.
</snippet>

Title: Flower strips as a carbon sequestration measure in temperate croplands
Snippet: For the first time, biomass of flower strips has been determined and analysed in relation to plant biodiversity. We found a significant negative correlation between the total number of unique plant species in the flower strip and its total biomass production, suggesting that highly diverse flower strips are less productive. The biomass of the flower strip is not harvested or removed, and thus flower strips have a much greater input of C to the soil compared to croplands. 

Additionally, the C sequestration potential of flower strips has also been modelled for the first time. We estimate that flower strips can sequester 0.48 Mg ± 0.36 C ha −1 year −1 in the initial 20 years after establishment in temperate, intensively used mineral soils. This rate is comparable to other C sequestrations methods, including cover crops and land use conversion to grassland. As with the total biomass, there is a negative correlation between C sequestration rate and biodiversity; thus there may be a trade-off between maximising plant biodiversity and C sequestration in flower strips.

If an additional 1 % of German cropland on mineral soils was converted to flower strips, an additional 0.065 Tg C would be sequestered in the soil, which corresponds to 0.4 % of all GHG emissions from the German agricultural sector. Converting cropland to flower strips is not a fail-safe C sequestration method. Areas with already-high inputs of organic C from organic fertilisers, including manure, and biomass will see a lower potential C sequestering effect of flower strips. Furthermore, only a permanent flower strip can act as a significant C sink for climate mitigation. However, flower strips often improve agricultural yields through increased pollinator attraction and pest predation and have synergistic relations with overall ecosystem biodiversity. Therefore, implementing flower strips as a simple and easy-to-implement management option by farmers can improve multiple critical agro-environmental issues simultaneously.
</snippet>

Title: Prairie Strips and Lower Land Use Intensity Increase Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
Snippet: This conservation practice consists of retiring areas of farmland and actively restoring them by seeding native perennial vegetation. Supported by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) Conservation Reserve Program (CRP), prairie strips are one of many "edge of field" practices-including riparian buffers, hedgerows, and wildflower strips-aimed at incorporating native and diverse habitat into agricultural landscapes (The Nature Conservancy [TNC], 2021). 

Once established, prairie strips in contoured farm landscapes can reduce soil erosion, improve water quality, and support biodiversity. This can provide benefits to the farm and farmer at disproportionately higher levels than the amount of farmland removed from production (Schulte et al., 2017). Prairie strips also have the potential to provide resources and habitat for beneficial insects and increase their spillover into the farm, where they can provide ecosystem services such as biocontrol and pollination (Blitzer et al., 2012;Morandin and Kremen, 2013;Kordbacheh et al., 2020). While prairie strips are known to benefit biodiversity and ecosystem services once they have been established for multiple years, these impacts have not been studied during their initial years of establishment. Measuring prairie strips' conservation potential during their early establishment period can address this gap and increase the precision of farmers' expectations of prairie strips. 

The conservation potential of prairie strips relative to other agricultural conservation practices such as no tillage is also unknown. Biodiversity and ecosystem services in agroecosystems are driven not only by the presence of natural habitat on or near farms, but also by the agricultural management practices used in row crop areas. Crop rotations and cover crops generally increase biodiversity and enhance nutrient availability (Rusch et al., 2013;de Pedro et al., 2020;Bowers et al., 2021), whereas the use of tillage, pesticides, and fertilizer generally decrease biodiversity and increase greenhouse gas emissions (Syswerda and Robertson, 2014;Bowles et al., 2016;Raven and Wagner, 2021).

Title: Carbon Balance of Pulse Crops in Rotation with Spring Wheat
Snippet: Carbon footprint and C balance are used to understand whether an agroecosystem is a C source or sink. Our objective was to evaluate C inputs and outputs for determining C balance for pulse crops in rotation with spring wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) from 2021 to 2022 to 2024–2025 in the US northern Great Plains. Pulse crops (chickpea [Cicer arietinum L], lentil [Lens culinaris Medik.], and pea [Pisum sativum L.]) were rotated with spring wheat to form four crop rotations (chickpea–spring wheat, lentil–spring wheat, pea–spring wheat, and spring wheat–spring wheat). Straw C was 26–74% lower for pulse crops than spring wheat, but 19–23% greater for pea–spring wheat than chickpea–spring wheat and lentil–spring wheat. Root biomass and rhizodeposit C were 24–31% greater for spring wheat–spring wheat than chickpea–spring wheat and pea–spring wheat. Grain C was 21% greater for pea than chickpea, but 64–97% lower for pulse crops than spring wheat. Cumulative CO2 flux from May to April was 14–17% greater for spring wheat–spring wheat than chickpea–spring wheat and lentil–spring wheat. Soil C sequestration rate was greater for pea and spring wheat than chickpea and lentil, or greater for pea–spring wheat and spring wheat–spring wheat than other crop rotations. Carbon balance was 5–16% lower for pulse crops than spring wheat, or 9–16% lower for pulse crop–spring wheat rotations than spring wheat–spring wheat. Because of greater C input and C sequestration rate, spring wheat can reduce C loss compared to pulse crops, or continuous spring wheat can reduce the loss compared to pulse crop–spring wheat rotations.
</snippet>

Title: Immediate and second‐year effects of preceding crops on wheat production in the Northern Great Plains
Snippet: Growers in the Northern Great Plains (NGP) are increasingly adopting winter wheat (WW; Triticum aestivum L.) into their crop rotations in years of ideal fall planting conditions due to its high yield potential. Our study evaluated WW responses to rotational crops, soybean (Glycine max L.) and lentil (Lens culinaris L.), field peas (Pisum sativum L.), faba bean (Vicia faba L.), canola (Brassica napus L.), flax (Linum usitatissimum L.), and oats (Avena sativa L.), and to different wheat rotational schemes following the rotational crop: WW‐WW, hard red spring wheat (HRSW)‐WW, and WW‐HRSW. Although canola is traditionally favored for its snow‐trapping benefits, soybean and lentil can achieve similar or superior results, enhancing both WW grain yields and protein concentrations when grown immediately after these two rotational crops. These benefits persisted in the second wheat phase in the WW–WW and HRSW–WW systems, albeit with increased variability. Canola stubble, while not offering immediate advantages for WW, contributed to high and stable yields in WW and HRSW when planted in the second year. However, a wheat yield drag was noted in the second year, especially affecting HRSW, indicating that monoculture cereal rotations are more detrimental to HRSW than to WW. In‐crop growth patterns aligned with yield responses, with leguminous stubbles, especially lentil, promoting superior in‐season growth compared to canola, flax, and oats. This study underscores WW as a viable option for cereal phases in the NGP cropping systems, contributing to enhanced ecological benefits in the local environment. By adopting WW in their cropping systems, growers can accrue synergistic benefits with multiple rotational crops.
</snippet>

Title: Herbivore-induced volatile emissions are altered by soil legacy effects in cereal cropping systems
Snippet: Soil was collected from the Northern Agriculture Research Center located south of Havre, MT (48°29'48.8"N, 109°48'10.4"W). The site is a waterlimited agroecosystem of the Northern Great Plains (NGP) with an average annual precipitation of 305 mm. Average annual high and low temperatures at the site are 13.6 and 0.0 °C, respectively (Western Regional Climate Center 2020). Since 2012, two replicate fields (40 m x 360 m, each) have been planted in an alternating rotation of winter wheat (Triticum aestivum L., Judee variety) with either cover crop mixtures or fallow (Fig. 1). Within each field, each treatment is randomly repeated in 3 separate plots (8 m x 14 m). The location of each treatment was randomized in 2012 and has been maintained through time. 

This study used inoculums of soil collected from low and high diversity cropping systems: (1) winter wheat rotated with fallow and (2) winter wheat rotated with a 7-species mixture of cover crops that was terminated by grazing cattle. Hereafter, soil from these cropping systems will be referred to as 'fallow inoculum' and 'cover crop inoculum', respectively. The cover crop mixture consisted of radish (Raphanus raphanistrum L.), lentil (Lens culinaris Medikus), field pea (Pisum sativum L.), oat (Avena sativa L.), turnip (Brassica rapa L.), sorghum x sudan grass (Sorghum drummondii Nees ex. 

Steud.), and soybean (Glycine max L.). Species were selected based on USDA-ARS recommendations for the NGP and represent a range of functional groups with potential for the provision of various ecosystem services (https://www.ars.usda.gov/plains-area/mandannd/ngprl/docs/cover-crop-chart/). Cover crop plots were planted mid-May and terminated early-July to protect soil moisture, as practiced in the region (O'Dea et al. 2013).

Title: Introducing cover crops as fallow replacement in the Northern Great Plains: II. Impact on following wheat crops
Snippet: The adoption of cover crops in replacement of fallow has been slow in the Northern Great Plains despite government incentives from American agencies. Reductions in wheat yields following cover crops were frequent enough and important enough to raise some concerns about their introduction in semi-arid cropping systems such as the Northern Great Plains. However, the previous year cover crop biomass was a poor predictor of wheat yields, whereas in-season rainfall explained more variability in wheat yields. Termination treatments did not significantly impact grain yield, soil nitrate or soil organic matter, which suggest the use of cover crops through grazing or hay could represent an economic benefit in this system. Further economic analyses are required to determine if the integration of livestock is necessary to mitigate the risks associated with the introduction of cover crops in replacement of fallow in the Northern Great Plains.
</snippet>

Title: Introducing cover crops as a fallow replacement in the Northern Great Plains: I. Evaluation of cover crop mixes as a forage source for grazing cattle
Snippet: This research was part of a long-term study evaluating cover crops in a semi-arid region of the Northern Great Plains. Research was conducted at the Montana State University-Northern Agricultural Research Center near Havre, MT (48°29 ′ N, −109°48 ′ W) from 2012 to 2019. The research site is approximately 815 m above sea level, with an average annual precipitation of 305 mm. Soil is characterized as clay loam and classified as a Telstad-Joplin complex. The site is characterized as having 129 frost-free days and an average annual temperature of 5.94°C with an average high of 13.6°C and average low of 0.0°C. Weather data were collected onsite with official National Weather Service (NOAA) meteorological instruments. Recorded monthly mean, maximum and minimum temperatures and precipitation for April, May, June and July 2012 through 2019 and long-term averages  are presented in Table 1. 

This experiment was conducted as a randomized-completeblock design, where 29 individual species were utilized in 15 different cover crop mixtures in a wheat-cover crop rotation (Table 2). Cover crop mixtures were classified into three treatment groups, including (1) cool-season species, (2) warm-season species and (3) cool-and warm-season species mixture (mid-season). Both the commodity crop (spring and winter wheat) and each of the 15 cover crop mixtures were present in each of two adjacent fields (three replications per field) for each year of the study (2012)(2013)(2014)(2015)(2016)(2017)(2018)(2019). The cover crop mixtures were randomly allotted to plots (7.3 by 40.2 m) within each field the first year of the study and each treatment was planted in the same plot for the remainder of the trial in a wheat-cover crop rotation.

Summary and framing
In semi-arid Northern Great Plains (NGP) cropping systems, agrobiodiversity interventions that stabilize yields in the short term—via pollinator support (floral strips, forage/seed mixes, mass-flowering crops) or annual pest regulation (habitat diversification, intercropping, cover crops that recruit natural enemies)—can conflict with long-term soil carbon (C) accumulation when they increase aboveground or rhizosphere C losses, favor C4 pathways with higher respiratory losses, or export biomass outside the field system. The direction and magnitude of soil C change depend on the balance of C inputs (residue and root inputs, rhizodeposits) and C losses (soil respiration, denigration/oxidation, export via grazing/harvest, and off-site transport). Evidence from NGP rotations, prairie/flower strips, and cover crop trials shows that some pollinator- and pest-support strategies boost biodiversity and ecosystem services with modest or early soil C gains, while others can reduce SOC or impose management costs that undermine long-term C storage. <cite id="f45b9a9e-2">Prairie strips increased soil organic carbon and biodiversity while maintaining yields in early years</cite><cite id="58f54fad-2">Mass-flowering legumes provide temporary floral resources and can reduce fertilizer needs but still sequester soil C at moderate rates in their early years</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-0">Leguminous pulses in rotation can reduce cumulative CO2 efflux and SOC sequestration relative to cereals, whereas continuous spring wheat or pea–wheat rotations sometimes accrue higher SOC</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-3">Flower strips that maximize plant diversity tend to be less productive and still add substantial C to soil, with permanent strips acting as significant C sinks</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-3">In NGP, grazing/hay termination of cover crops often showed no significant change in SOC in the second year</cite>.

Pollinator-support interventions: when short-term stability conflicts with long-term SOC
- Mechanisms of short-term stability: sequential and mass-flowering crops, floral strips, and hedgerows increase spatio-temporal continuity and abundance of pollinators, boosting pollination services and biocontrol spillover into cropland; these effects are robust across semi-arid and temperate contexts. <cite id="58f54fad-4">Increasing landscape complexity via intercropping, cover crops, and crop-livestock mixtures increases floral resources and habitat for pollinators and stabilizes pollinator communities</cite><cite id="58f54fad-2">Annual flowering fields (mass-flowering legumes/beans) raise pollinator abundance and species richness, and can fix N, but still deliver C sequestration via residue inputs to soil</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-0">Prairie strips concentrated litter inputs near edges and showed subtle but detectable increases in “active carbon” adjacent to strips in the first post-mowing year</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-1">Prairie strips and reduced land-use intensity increased pollination, butterflies, spiders, and dung beetles with clear spillover gradients</cite>.
- Conflicts with long-term SOC:
  1) Biomass removal and export: when floral/forage strips are harvested for seed or silage, or when cover crops are taken as hay/forage, added C is removed from the system, lowering net SOC accumulation. <cite id="f45b9a9e-3">Flower strips not harvested have much greater C input to soil than croplands; areas with high external organic C inputs (manure/biomass) show lower incremental C sequestration, and only permanent strips act as significant C sinks</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-3">Termination by grazing or hay showed no significant change in SOC in the second year, suggesting that when biomass is removed, C gains are offset and require economic integration to be viable</cite>. In semi-arid rotations, legumes like lentils and chickpeas produce less straw C than wheat and can reduce cumulative CO2 efflux and SOC accrual compared to cereals, highlighting that “temporary” floral pulses may add pollinator services but reduce residue-driven SOC inputs. <cite id="b31e37fd-0">Straw C was 26–74% lower for pulses than spring wheat; root biomass and rhizodeposits were 24–31% lower for pulse–wheat than wheat–wheat; SOC sequestration rate was greater for pea and spring wheat than chickpea/lentil, or greater for pea–wheat than other rotations</cite>.
  2) High-diversity, low-biomass strips: maximizing plant species richness reduces total biomass production, which can lower direct C inputs even as it supports pollinator richness. <cite id="f45b9a9e-3">A significant negative correlation between unique plant species and total biomass in flower strips indicates that highly diverse strips are less productive, yet still have greater C input than cropland; there is a trade-off between maximizing biodiversity and C sequestration in flower strips</cite>.
  3) C4 pulse dominance and respiratory losses: pulses (C4) often have higher photosynthetic rates but greater respiratory CO2 efflux; in rotations, this can reduce net C storage relative to C3 cereals when pulses replace cereals in cereal phases. <cite id="b31e37fd-0">Cumulative CO2 flux from May to April was 14–17% greater for continuous spring wheat than pulse–wheat rotations; SOC sequestration rates are higher for pea and spring wheat than chickpea and lentil</cite>. In NGP rotations, soybean and lentil improved subsequent wheat yields and protein, yet the cereal phase’s replacement by legumes reduced net C inputs and SOC gains compared to wheat-only rotations. <cite id="b31e37fd-1">Soybean and lentil grown immediately before wheat enhanced yields and protein; however, rotation dynamics showed cereal phases benefit ecological processes, and leguminous stubbles altered growth trajectories</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-0">Pulse–wheat rotations had 5–16% lower carbon balance than wheat–wheat, indicating greater C loss or lower net sequestration</cite>.
  4) Off-site export and wind/ice damage: tall, dense floral/forage strips and grassed waterways can increase litter and herbivory pressure and create disservices like herbivory drag; if biomass is periodically mowed or grazed and exported, net C inputs decline. <cite id="f45b9a9e-0">Prairie strips increased active carbon near edges; mowing in 2019 caused a spillover of prairie litter inputs into cropland, highlighting biogeochemical benefits and potential disservices like herbivory that were not measured</cite>.
- Management choices that create the tradeoff:
  - Annual mass-flowering forage crops (e.g., clovers, peas) used as seed/forage: deliver short-term pollinator stability and N fixation but, when harvested, remove C that would otherwise accrue in soil; risk higher in arid years when inputs are limited and residues are small. <cite id="58f54fad-2">Legumes provide ample temporary food resources for pollinators and reduce fertilizer demand; their C inputs contribute to soil C accrual when left in place</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-3">Only permanent flower strips act as significant C sinks; high external inputs reduce incremental C gains</cite>.
  - High-diversity wildflower strips sown as temporary habitat: enhance pollinator richness and stability but often reduce total biomass; net C addition to soil exists, yet the per-area C sequestration rate can be lower than lower-diversity, higher-biomass strips. <cite id="f45b9a9e-3">More species correlate with less total biomass, with modeled C sequestration ~0.48 Mg C ha−1 year−1 in early years; trade-off between biodiversity and C accrual</cite>.
  - Pulses replacing cereal phases in rotations: improve yield stability and protein but reduce SOC sequestration relative to cereals due to lower straw/root C and higher respiratory losses; in NGP, this can appear as improved agronomic stability without commensurate long-term C gain. <cite id="b31e37fd-0">Pulse–wheat rotations had lower SOC sequestration rates than wheat–wheat; continuous wheat or pea–wheat sometimes accrue more SOC</cite>.
  - Livestock integration with cover/forage strips: grazing can convert C inputs to animal products with local feed value; hay/seed removal likewise departs the system. When properly integrated, these systems can maintain or improve SOC due to persistent litter and reduced tillage, but when biomass is repeatedly exported, SOC gains are limited. <cite id="b31e37fd-3">Termination by grazing or hay did not significantly change SOC in the second year but suggested economic benefits via forage, implying that livestock integration can mitigate risks of replacing fallow</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-4">Prairie strips reduce erosion and support biodiversity; cover crops and reduced tillage generally increase biodiversity and nutrient availability, whereas tillage and pesticides decrease biodiversity and increase GHG emissions</cite>.

Pest-regulation interventions: when short-term stability conflicts with long-term SOC
- Mechanisms of short-term stability: habitat diversification (hedgerows, field borders, intercropping), cover crops, and crop-livestock mixtures recruit and sustain natural enemies and reduce pest outbreaks; these practices increase floral and nesting resources and habitat connectivity, stabilizing yields via biocontrol. <cite id="58f54fad-4">Increasing habitat complexity and connectivity through hedgerows, cover crops, and polyculture systems promotes wild pollinator diversity and stability</cite><cite id="58f54fad-1">Floral resource diversity and abundance in diversified horticultural systems support comparable pollinator richness and abundance to semi-natural grasslands, complementing specialized habitats</cite>.
- Conflicts with long-term SOC:
  1) Increased standing biomass and herbivory: diversified pest-regulation habitats often increase aboveground productivity and insect community complexity, which can elevate herbivory and disease pressure; when these pressures are managed with herbicides or fungicides, input-induced C emissions offset soil C gains. <cite id="58f54fad-0">Diversification improves heterogeneity and connectivity for pollinators but requires long-term study on crops to diversify with and how landscape context modulates effects</cite><cite id="58f54fad-3">Land-use changes alter pollinator communities with consequences for plant fitness; mass flowering crops can mediate pollinator spatial distribution, affecting plant–pollinator and plant–herbivore dynamics</cite>. In semi-arid NGP, cover crops terminated by grazing/hay showed no immediate SOC change; persistent biomass and increased pest pressure can drive growers toward inputs that raise net C losses. <cite id="b31e37fd-3">Cover crops as fallow replacement often showed no significant change in SOC in the second year, with termination method not significantly impacting SOC, underscoring the need for economic/livestock integration to mitigate risk</cite>.
  2) Carbon losses via denigration/oxidation of fine roots and rhizodeposits under stress: diversified systems with high root exudation can increase microbial activity; under semi-arid stress, pulses (C4) and certain intercropping combinations elevate respiratory CO2, reducing net C storage despite increased belowground inputs. <cite id="b31e37fd-0">Root biomass and rhizodeposits were 24–31% greater for wheat–wheat than pulse–wheat, yet cumulative CO2 flux was 14–17% greater in continuous wheat; SOC sequestration rates favored cereals over C4 pulses</cite>.
  3) Timing and precipitation variability: in semi-arid systems, pest-regulation benefits are highly weather-dependent. Intercrops and cover crops may suppress early-season pests but can also compete with the cash crop, lowering first-year yields; when moisture is poor, termination by grazing/hay diverts C away from soil, and any SOC gains are delayed or negated. <cite id="b31e37fd-1">Canola stubble did not offer immediate wheat yield advantages but supported high and stable yields in subsequent years; monoculture cereal rotations were more detrimental to hard red spring wheat than to winter wheat, highlighting crop- and phase-specific tradeoffs</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-2">At a 305 mm precipitation site in Montana, alternating wheat with cover crop mixtures (radish, lentil, pea, oat, turnip, sorghum-sudangrass, soybean) was practiced to protect soil moisture; this context underscores how functional groups are adopted to deliver multiple services</cite>.
- Management choices that create the tradeoff:
  - Annual intercropping with pest-suppressive legumes (e.g., soybean–wheat) for insurance: improves early-season pest regulation and nutrient complementarity but can reduce SOC inputs compared to cereal intercrops and increase risk of herbivory and disease requiring inputs. <cite id="b31e37fd-1">Soybean and lentil immediately prior to wheat enhanced yields and protein; their stubbles supported superior in-season growth, illustrating ecological benefits alongside potential for increased pest pressure</cite>.
  - Herbaceous borders and wildflower strips adjacent to cash crops: increase natural enemy diversity and pollination services but can increase herbivory disservices; if managed with frequent herbicide applications to suppress weeds and pests, net C sink potential declines. <cite id="58f54fad-0">Outstanding questions include which crops to diversify with and how farming intensity modulates effects on pollinators</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-0">Prairie strips spillover benefits included active carbon near edges; potential ecosystem disservices like herbivory were noted and warrant study</cite>.
  - Cover crops sown as forage/hay in semi-arid rotations: deliver short-term soil protection and moisture retention but often show no immediate SOC change when terminated; if biomass is exported, net SOC can decline. Economic integration with grazing reduces this export and can maintain SOC via persistent litter and reduced tillage. <cite id="b31e37fd-3">Termination treatments did not significantly impact SOC in the second year, suggesting cover crops can be integrated as forage to add economic value while preserving or improving SOC with proper management</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-4">Cover crops and reduced till generally increase biodiversity and nutrient availability, whereas tillage and pesticides decrease biodiversity and increase GHG emissions</cite>.

When and where the conflict arises in NGP practice
- Early vs. late season and multi-year dynamics: Pollinator-support via prairie/flower strips accrues measurable SOC near edges within 1–3 years in NGP-like semi-arid settings, especially under lower land-use intensity; however, first-year mowing or biomass export reverses this by removing litter inputs, creating a short-term stability (forage/seed) vs. long-term SOC tradeoff. <cite id="f45b9a9e-2">Soil organic carbon and multiple biodiversity metrics increased with reduced land use intensity; benefits spilled over within 1–3 years</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-0">Mowing strips in 2019 caused a spillover of prairie litter into cropland in adjacent sites, highlighting that management timing and disturbance alter C inputs</cite>.
- Crop identity and phase: Replacing cereal phases with legumes (e.g., lentil–wheat or continuous legumes) improves agronomic stability via N fixation and diverse blooms but reduces net SOC compared to cereals due to lower straw/root C and higher respiration; conversely, continuous cereals or pea–wheat rotations often accrue higher SOC, creating a tradeoff between pest-suppressive legumes and long-term C storage. <cite id="b31e37fd-0">Pulse–wheat rotations had 5–16% lower carbon balance than wheat–wheat; root biomass and rhizodeposits were lower in pulses; SOC sequestration favored cereals</cite>.
- Intensification and inputs: Pest-regulation through diversified habitats can spur herbivory and disease, pushing farmers toward inputs (herbicides/fungicides) that increase net GHGs and erode SOC benefits; this is particularly acute in semi-arid years when moisture stress reduces cereal competitiveness and prompts more intensive management. <cite id="58f54fad-0">Designing long-term studies on how crop diversification benefits wild pollinators remains essential; farming intensity and landscape context modulate effects</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-3">Second-year SOC showed no significant change with cover crops, emphasizing the need for economic/livestock integration to mitigate risks</cite>.
- Spatial configuration and permanence: Temporary, high-diversity floral strips add C but at lower per-area rates; permanent native prairie strips and native perennial borders act as stronger C sinks and stabilize multiple services, reducing conflict by embedding C in long-lived soil pools. <cite id="f45b9a9e-3">Flower strips not harvested add substantial C to soil; only permanent strips act as significant C sinks; more species correlate with less biomass and modeled C sequestration</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-2">Prairie strips increased SOC and biodiversity with reduced land use intensity, with benefits spilling over into cropland</cite>.

Management levers to align short-term stability with long-term SOC in NGP
- Prefer native prairie strips and perennial borders over annual wildflower seed mixes where feasible: native, perennial systems build SOC faster and provide persistent habitat, reducing biomass export and herbivory drag; integrate livestock grazing to recycle nutrients in situ rather than removing hay/seed. <cite id="f45b9a9e-2">Prairie strips increased SOC and ecosystem services early in establishment and with reduced land-use intensity</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-3">Permanent flower strips are significant C sinks; high external inputs reduce incremental gains</cite>.
- Use cereal-dominant rotations with targeted floral intercrops or late-season “green manure” phases: cereal phases increase residue C and SOC accrual; insert legumes or brassicas as short-duration pest-regulation or pollinator-support phases only when moisture supports them, then terminate and graze to keep C local. <cite id="b31e37fd-0">Wheat–wheat or pea–wheat rotations accrue higher SOC than pulse–wheat; SOC sequestration is greater for cereals</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-1">Legumes immediately prior to wheat enhanced yields and protein; cereal phases can leverage ecological benefits while maintaining residue inputs</cite>.
- Design floral and habitat strips for high C retention: favor lower-diversity, higher-biomass mixes or shorter-duration sow–terminate–graze rotations; place strips on wind-exposed edges to reduce aboveground loss, and avoid mowing unless needed for weed control. <cite id="f45b9a9e-3">More species correlate with less biomass and a trade-off between biodiversity and C sequestration; modeled C accrual ~0.48 Mg C ha−1 year−1 early years</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-0">Mowing prairie strips altered litter spillover and active carbon near edges, underscoring management timing effects</cite>.
- Tighten pest-regulation design to minimize herbivory: select intercrops and borders with complementary phenology and pest repulsion, maintain competitive cereals in dry years, and use thresholds-based IPM to avoid blanket herbicide that erodes SOC. <cite id="b31e37fd-2">Cover crop mixes in NGP were selected for multiple ecosystem services, reflecting functional group complementarity under water-limited conditions</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-1">Monoculture cereal rotations were more detrimental to hard red spring wheat than to winter wheat, emphasizing crop-specific ecological tradeoffs</cite>.
- Weather- and phase-tailor habitat strategies: in canola-dominant rotations, retain stubble and delay termination to preserve residue C; in legume-heavy phases, compensate for lower SOC by boosting cereal follow-on crops and using reduced till to maximize residue retention. <cite id="b31e37fd-1">Canola stubble supported high and stable yields in subsequent wheat and HRSW when planted; monoculture cereal rotations were more detrimental to HRSW than WW</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-4">Reduced tillage generally increases biodiversity and nutrient availability; tillage and pesticides increase GHG emissions</cite>.
- Recognize the role of plant metabolism: avoid long-term dominance by C4 legumes where SOC accrual is the goal; sequence C4 pulses to pest-prone early spring windows, then terminate and reincorporate into cereal phases that favor SOC. <cite id="b31e37fd-0">Pulses have higher cumulative CO2 efflux and lower SOC sequestration rates than cereals; continuous wheat or pea–wheat often outpace pulses in SOC accrual</cite>.

Practical takeaways for NGP farmers and advisors
- Conflict windows: The clearest conflicts occur when pollinator- or pest-support biomass is harvested (seed/forage/hay), when legumes replace cereal phases for extended periods, or when diversified habitats trigger herbicide/fungicide escalation. <cite id="f45b9a9e-3">Biomass removal reduces incremental SOC; only permanent habitat acts as a strong C sink</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-0">Pulse–wheat rotations had lower SOC sequestration than wheat–wheat</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-3">Second-year SOC effects of cover crops were minimal when terminated by grazing/hay, indicating potential for economic integration to maintain SOC</cite>.
- Win–win windows: Early establishment of native prairie strips and native perennial borders under reduced tillage; cereal–cover crop rotations with on-farm grazing; and polyculture sequences that ensure floral continuity without biomass export. <cite id="f45b9a9e-2">Prairie strips increased SOC and biodiversity under reduced land-use intensity with early benefits</cite><cite id="f45b9a9e-4">Cover crops and reduced tillage increase biodiversity and nutrient cycling while limiting GHGs</cite>.
- Measurement and planning: Quantify enterprise-level gains from pollination/pest control and livestock forage against SOC accrual goals; sequence rotations to use high-SOC cereal phases as anchors, and deploy legumes/flower strips strategically. <cite id="b31e37fd-1">Adopting winter wheat into cereal phases can accrue synergistic ecological benefits with multiple rotational crops</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-0">Rotation choice measurably shifts C balance and SOC sequestration rates</cite>.

Bottom line
In semi-arid NGP cropping, pollinator-support and annual pest-regulation interventions that deliver short-term stability often conflict with long-term soil C accumulation when they export biomass, favor C4 pulses with higher respiratory losses, or trigger input-intensive management; the tradeoff is strongest for annual forage/seed floral strips, high-diversity low-biomass mixes, and legume-heavy rotations. Aligning goals requires permanent native habitat, cereal-dominant SOC phases, targeted floral and pest-regulation strips sited for C retention, and livestock integration to keep biomass cycling on-farm. <cite id="f45b9a9e-3">Flower strips add C when left permanent and unharvested, with modeled early-year sequestration comparable to cover crops and grassland conversion</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-0">Cereal-based rotations and pea–wheat generally accrue higher SOC than pulse–wheat due to greater residue inputs and lower efflux</cite><cite id="b31e37fd-3">When cover crops are grazed or harvested for hay, SOC changes are minimal in the short term, but economic and management integration are needed to avoid net C loss</cite>.</answer>

Title: Crop diversification for pollinator conservation
Snippet: Crop diversification has gained momentum because of the many benefits it can have for farmers and the environment (Tamburini et al. 2020;Beillouin et al. 2021;Nicholson and Williams 2021). Crop fields are not as stable and diverse as natural habitats, and cannot replace the importance of semi-natural habitat for pollinator conservation (Batáry et al. 2015;Eeraerts 2023;Fijen et al. 2024), we highlight the potential of crop diversification practices as an additional pollinator conservation measure (Table 1; Fig. 2). Crop diversification can enhance spatio-temporal flower resource availability, continuity and accessibility without too drastic adjustments for farmers, while also improving the landscape heterogeneity and functional connectivity for pollinators. With large changes ahead in the agricultural system driven by climate change and the need for a more plant-based diet, it is essential to design long-term studies on how crop diversification can benefit wild pollinators. Outstanding questions include what crops to diversify with, and how landscape context and farming intensity can modulate the effect on crop diversification practices on wild pollinators. Combined effects of multiple crop diversification practices on wild pollinators are also virtually unknown. Crop diversification with both agricultural production and pollinator conservation in mind can provide synergies without taking a substantial part of land out of production: after all, farmers need pollinators for high yields of many crops (Turo et al. 2024)

Title: Small-scale, diverse horticultural systems and semi-natural grasslands support complementary pollinator populations
Snippet: Pollinating insects are of great importance in natural ecosystems and agricultural landscapes. Despite their crucial role for food production, safeguarding pollination services is becoming increasingly challenging due to pollinator declines. Habitat loss and agricultural intensification are among the main drivers, causing a substantial reduction in the availability of floral resources. Despite efforts, the uptake of measures to halt these declines in agricultural landscapes is low. Implementation of a novel crop production system is therefore proposed as a solution to ensure food security whilst concomitantly minimising environmental degradation and the associated biodiversity loss. Agricultural diversification is one such strategy that is known to promote multiple ecosystem services. Yet, the effects of agricultural diversification on pollinator populations in farm-scale, observational studies remains understudied. Here, we examine the importance of small-scale, diverse horticultural systems (SDHS) to support wild pollinator communities. Floral resources and wild pollinators were sampled in both SDHSs and semi-natural grasslands (SNG) in 16 landscapes in Flanders, Belgium. During late summer, these SNGs provide and important source of floral resources, thereby serving as a benchmark habitat to which the SDHSs are compared. Our study highlights the value of SDHSs as they provide diverse and abundant floral resources compared to SNGs. Moreover, pollinator species richness and abundance were comparable between the two habitats. Conversely, floral resource and pollinator community composition differed, indicating that different pollinator communities used the complementary resources provided by both habitat types. Furthermore, we show that SNGs represent the most specialised habitat type. We therefore argue that SDHSs can be considered to be an additional, complementary source of floral resources to those provided by SNGs. However, these SDHSs cannot substitute SNGs, given the importance of these grasslands for pollinators.

Title: No evidence of decline in bumblebee abundance and species richness from edge to interior in moderately-sized red clover fields
Snippet: Agricultural intensification and associated changes in land use have substantially decreased local biodiversity (Ramankutty et al. 2008;Jaureguiberry et al. 2022). Such declines in biodiversity directly influence a wide range of ecosystem functions, ultimately impacting both the remaining natural habitats as well as agricultural fields. For instance, intensified agriculture reduces resources available to pollinators, leading to lower pollinator abundance and species richness within agricultural landscapes (Potts et al. 2010;Dupont et al. 2011;Goulson et al. 2015). In turn, the decrease in pollinator populations can lead to insufficient pollination, ultimately reducing crop yields (Garibaldi et al. 2009;Jing et al. 2021). 

To persist in agricultural landscapes, wild pollinators need appropriate nesting and foraging sites, which are scarce in intensively managed fields. Enhancing habitat diversity within agricultural areas has been suggested as a way to mitigate this limitation and improve pollination services provided by wild pollinators (e.g., Potts et al. 2016;Garibaldi et al. 2021). Such diversification measures include floral enhancements along field margins (e.g., hedgerows or wildflower plantings), adding natural habitat features at the landscape level (e.g., increasing the proportion of natural vegetation cover), and cultivating massflowering crops that provide forage for pollinators. 

One of the most widely adopted practices to mitigate the effects of intensive agriculture and support wild pollinators is the cultivation of annual flowering fields. In the European Union, this measure is included in the mandatory agri-environmental schemes under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP). Under these schemes, farmers are subsidized for managing their land for the benefit of natural habitats and species, including through intercropping. The mass-flowering crops cultivated in these annual flowering fields include legumes, such as clovers and beans. Legumes provide ample, albeit temporary, food resources for many pollinating insects, thereby increasing their abundance and species richness in agroecosystems. Additionally, they enhance soil fertility through nitrogen fixation, reducing the need for synthetic fertilizers, and they can be harvested for seeds and silage.

Title: Human-Mediated Land Use Change Drives Intraspecific Plant Trait Variation
Snippet: Because many pollinators utilize both wild plants and crops, sharing local pollinators creates potential fitness implications through interference in visitation rates or pollen transfer (Stanley and Stout, 2014). For example, mass blooming crops can mediate the spatial distribution of pollinators in the landscape, reducing visitation and fitness in coblooming wild plants (Holzschuh et al., 2011;Van Reeth et al., 2019). Conversely, mass crop blooms may augment pollinator populations, increasing spillover and boosting the fitness of wild plants blooming immediately after the crop (Kovács-Hostyánszki et al., 2013). Therefore, mass flowering crops can have opposing outcomes for wild plant populations via separate mechanisms suggesting that the kind of habitat conversion as well as the traits of focal wild plant populations are likely to have strong impacts on the outcome of these land use changes on wild plant populations. 

In some systems, plants demonstrate resilience to land use change. This is exemplified when there is no detectable effect of land use change on plant reproductive success (Lopes and Buzato, 2007;Ekroos et al., 2015;Skogen et al., 2016;Grass et al., 2018) likely because these landscapes select for pollinator species that are tolerant to disturbance and/or have a high dispersal ability. In restored prairies, increasing proportion of agriculture in the surrounding landscape did not increase pollen limitation in a pollinator dependent forb (Ritchie et al., 2020). It is possible that the restored prairies provide habitat to support sufficient pollinators to prevent pollen limitation. Further, conflicting pressures of pollinators and herbivores could also be responsible for the failure of these studies to detect a fitness effect of landscape composition (Steffan-Dewenter et al., 2001). 

In summary, land use changes have substantial impacts on the composition of pollinator communities with potential consequences on plant fitness in remaining natural habitat fragments. As a rule, loss of natural habitat is expected to reduce the abundance and diversity of wild plant pollinators and consequently cause pollen limitation in wild plants (Taki et al., 2007); yet, exceptions to this rule, such as temporal effects of mass flowering crops, will alter these dynamics.

Title: Ecological intensification to mitigate impacts of conventional intensive land use on pollinators and pollination
Snippet: For example, Sardiñas et al. (2016) found that groundnesting native bees nested both within fields and edges, and that due to short actual foraging distances, visitation by bees nesting in and around fields led to a patchy distribution of pollination services across the field. 

Taking this knowledge into consideration, and within the ecological intensification framework (Table 1), restored or maintained semi-natural ecosystems, field border plantings and riparian buffer strips, can directly increase the complexity and connectivity of agricultural landscapes, often improving floral and nesting resources for pollinator diversity (Lagerl€ of et al. 1992;Carvell et al. 2004;Cole et al. 2015;Kremen & M'Gonigle 2015;Baude et al. 2016;Ponisio et al. 2016). Optimising management of these semi-natural areas, such as by adjusting mowing frequency and rotation, can diversify flower and insect pollinator communities (Noordijk et al. 2009;Halbritter et al. 2015) across the landscape. 

Increasing landscape complexity by employing crop and crop-livestock mixtures, intercropping and cover crops can increase floral resources and habitat for many pollinator species, even in landscapes with little semi-natural land-cover types (Williams & Kremen 2007;Bat ary et al. 2011;Kennedy et al. 2013). Increasing connectivity by reducing distances between foraging resources elevates pollinator diversity and abundance in fields (Ricketts et al. 2008;Kennedy et al. 2013;Clough et al. 2014). Diversified agricultural systems typified by a large number of crop types and small field sizes (Fahrig et al. 2015) promote wild pollinator diversity, community stability and pollination success of crops and wild plants ( Kremen & Miles 2012;Kennedy et al. 2013). Polyculture systems with sequentially flowering or co-flowering crops assure efficient pollination of plants differing in flower phenology by providing seasonal and spatial continuity of food resources supporting pollinator diversity and abundance (Mayfield & Belavadi 2008;Rundl€ of et al. 2014;Ponisio et al. 2015).

Further, conflicting pressures of pollinators and herbivores could also be responsible for the failure of these studies to detect a fitness effect of landscape composition (Steffan-Dewenter et al., 2001). 

In summary, land use changes have substantial impacts on the composition of pollinator communities with potential consequences on plant fitness in remaining natural habitat fragments. As a rule, loss of natural habitat is expected to reduce the abundance and diversity of wild plant pollinators and consequently cause pollen limitation in wild plants (Taki et al., 2007); yet, exceptions to this rule, such as temporal effects of mass flowering crops, will alter these dynamics.

Taking this knowledge into consideration, and within the ecological intensification framework (Table 1), restored or maintained semi-natural ecosystems, field border plantings and riparian buffer strips, can directly increase the complexity and connectivity of agricultural landscapes, often improving floral and nesting resources for pollinator diversity (Lagerl€ of et al. 1992;Carvell et al. 2004;Cole et al. 2015;Kremen & M'Gonigle 2015;Baude et al. 2016;Ponisio et al. 2016). Optimising management of these semi-natural areas, such as by adjusting mowing frequency and rotation, can diversify flower and insect pollinator communities (Noordijk et al. 2009;Halbritter et al. 2015) across the landscape. 

Increasing landscape complexity by employing crop and crop-livestock mixtures, intercropping and cover crops can increase floral resources and habitat for many pollinator species, even in landscapes with little semi-natural land-cover types (Williams & Kremen 2007;Bat ary et al. 2011;Kennedy et al. 2013). Increasing connectivity by reducing distances between foraging resources elevates pollinator diversity and abundance in fields (Ricketts et al. 2008;Kennedy et al. 2013;Clough et al. 2014). Diversified agricultural systems typified by a large number of crop types and small field sizes (Fahrig et al. 2015) promote wild pollinator diversity, community stability and pollination success of crops and wild plants ( Kremen & Miles 2012;Kennedy et al. 2013). Polyculture systems with sequentially flowering or co-flowering crops assure efficient pollination of plants differing in flower phenology by providing seasonal and spatial continuity of food resources supporting pollinator diversity and abundance (Mayfield & Belavadi 2008;Rundl€ of et al. 2014;Ponisio et al. 2015).

documents.title: Crop diversification for pollinator conservation
documents.snippet: Crop diversification has gained momentum because of the many benefits it can have for farmers and the environment (Tamburini et al. 2020;Beillouin et al. 2021;Nicholson and Williams 2021). Crop fields are not as stable and diverse as natural habitats, and cannot replace the importance of semi-natural habitat for pollinator conservation (Batáry et al. 2015;Eeraerts 2023;Fijen et al. 2024), we highlight the potential of crop diversification practices as an additional pollinator conservation measure (Table 1; Fig. 2). Crop diversification can enhance spatio-temporal flower resource availability, continuity and accessibility without too drastic adjustments for farmers, while also improving the landscape heterogeneity and functional connectivity for pollinators. With large changes ahead in the agricultural system driven by climate change and the need for a more plant-based diet, it is essential to design long-term studies on how crop diversification can benefit wild pollinators. Outstanding questions include what crops to diversify with, and how landscape context and farming intensity can modulate the effect on crop diversification practices on wild pollinators. Combined effects of multiple crop diversification practices on wild pollinators are also virtually unknown. Crop diversification with both agricultural production and pollinator conservation in mind can provide synergies without taking a substantial part of land out of production: after all, farmers need pollinators for high yields of many crops (Turo et al. 2024)

documents.title: Small-scale, diverse horticultural systems and semi-natural grasslands support complementary pollinator populations
documents.snippet: Pollinating insects are of great importance in natural ecosystems and agricultural landscapes. Despite their crucial role for food production, safeguarding pollination services is becoming increasingly challenging due to pollinator declines. Habitat loss and agricultural intensification are among the main drivers, causing a substantial reduction in the availability of floral resources. Despite efforts, the uptake of measures to halt these declines in agricultural landscapes is low. Implementation of a novel crop production system is therefore proposed as a solution to ensure food security whilst concomitantly minimising environmental degradation and the associated biodiversity loss. Agricultural diversification is one such strategy that is known to promote multiple ecosystem services. Yet, the effects of agricultural diversification on pollinator populations in farm-scale, observational studies remains understudied. Here, we examine the importance of small-scale, diverse horticultural systems (SDHS) to support wild pollinator communities. Floral resources and wild pollinators were sampled in both SDHSs and semi-natural grasslands (SNG) in 16 landscapes in Flanders, Belgium. During late summer, these SNGs provide and important source of floral resources, thereby serving as a benchmark habitat to which the SDHSs are compared. Our study highlights the value of SDHSs as they provide diverse and abundant floral resources compared to SNGs. Moreover, pollinator species richness and abundance were comparable between the two habitats. Conversely, floral resource and pollinator community composition differed, indicating that different pollinator communities used the complementary resources provided by both habitat types. Furthermore, we show that SNGs represent the most specialised habitat type. We therefore argue that SDHSs can be considered to be an additional, complementary source of floral resources to those provided by SNGs. However, these SDHSs cannot substitute SNGs, given the importance of these grasslands for pollinators.

documents.title: No evidence of decline in bumblebee abundance and species richness from edge to interior in moderately-sized red clover fields
documents.snippet:
Agricultural intensification and associated changes in land use have substantially decreased local biodiversity (Ramankutty et al. 2008;Jaureguiberry et al. 2022). Such declines in biodiversity directly influence a wide range of ecosystem functions, ultimately impacting both the remaining natural habitats as well as agricultural fields. For instance, intensified agriculture reduces resources available to pollinators, leading to lower pollinator abundance and species richness within agricultural landscapes (Potts et al. 2010;Dupont et al. 2011;Goulson et al. 2015). In turn, the decrease in pollinator populations can lead to insufficient pollination, ultimately reducing crop yields (Garibaldi et al. 2009;Jing et al. 2021). 

To persist in agricultural landscapes, wild pollinators need appropriate nesting and foraging sites, which are scarce in intensively managed fields. Enhancing habitat diversity within agricultural areas has been suggested as a way to mitigate this limitation and improve pollination services provided by wild pollinators (e.g., Potts et al. 2016;Garibaldi et al. 2021). Such diversification measures include floral enhancements along field margins (e.g., hedgerows or wildflower plantings), adding natural habitat features at the landscape level (e.g., increasing the proportion of natural vegetation cover), and cultivating massflowering crops that provide forage for pollinators. 

One of the most widely adopted practices to mitigate the effects of intensive agriculture and support wild pollinators is the cultivation of annual flowering fields. In the European Union, this measure is included in the mandatory agri-environmental schemes under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP). Under these schemes, farmers are subsidized for managing their land for the benefit of natural habitats and species, including through intercropping. The mass-flowering crops cultivated in these annual flowering fields include legumes, such as clovers and beans. Legumes provide ample, albeit temporary, food resources for many pollinating insects, thereby increasing their abundance and species richness in agroecosystems. Additionally, they enhance soil fertility through nitrogen fixation, reducing the need for synthetic fertilizers, and they can be harvested for seeds and silage.

documents.title: Human-Mediated Land Use Change Drives Intraspecific Plant Trait Variation
documents.snippet:
Because many pollinators utilize both wild plants and crops, sharing local pollinators creates potential fitness implications through interference in visitation rates or pollen transfer (Stanley and Stout, 2014). Snippet: We were surprised that prairie strips increased pollination as our plot sizes are a fraction of pollinator foraging range (Ricketts et al., 2008), and we suspect that pollinators were attracted to the high concentration of resources that contrasted strongly with crops. For active carbon, the effect of distance from prairie strip may have been driven by high prairie litter inputs. Mowing prairie strips in 2019 may have caused a spillover of prairie litter inputs into cropland that did not occur in 2020, leading to higher levels of active carbon in crop soils immediately adjacent to prairie strips. While the increase of active carbon in nearby sites was subtle, it still highlights the biogeochemical benefits of adjacent prairies for agricultural lands, which are generally underappreciated (Pérez-Suárez et al., 2014). 

Our study shows that spillover effects from prairie strips extend across measures of biodiversity and ecosystem services. Pollinators and pollination services have been studied at distances from restorations and habitat edges, often with higher numbers of pollinators and rates of pollination near non-crop habitat (Ricketts, 2004;Carvalheiro et al., 2010;Kordbacheh et al., 2020); by also demonstrating this phenomenon in dung beetles, spiders, active carbon, and decomposition, we show that these spatial effects apply to a broader array of organisms and ecosystem services. These results, with detailed attention to mechanism in our controlled experiment, strengthen evidence that suggests that strategic placement and amount of natural habitat in agricultural landscapes can add both conservation value and ecosystem services to an agricultural landscape (Basso et al., 2019;Mitchell et al., 2021). Our study focused on ecosystem services, and we did not measure potential ecosystem disservices from prairie strips that could impact yield, such as herbivory, however, such disservices could be addressed in future studies. 

Prairie strips require several years after planting to resemble a restored prairie community, over which time diversity and ecosystem services have been shown to accrue (Kurtz, 2013;Griffin et al., 2017). Title: Prairie Strips and Lower Land Use Intensity Increase Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
Snippet: We show that prairie strips, even early in their establishment, combined with lower land use intensity can promote biodiversity and ecosystem services without compromising crop yield. Within reduced input and biologically based treatments, where sampling effort occurred within prairie strips and at increasing distance from strips, biodiversity and ecosystem services spilled over into agronomic areas for five out of six measures. Among all treatments, using data from the entire plot area (not sampling within prairie strips for treatments with strips), pollination services and the abundance of butterflies and spiders were higher in plots with prairie strips. In addition, soil organic carbon, butterfly richness, and spider richness increased with a decrease in land use intensity. Crop yield in the reduced input treatment was equal to that of conventional management, even while including the area taken out of production. These effects were evident early in strip establishment, during which prairie strip plant communities changed from mostly weeds to a diversity of planted species. We expect the effects of strips to grow over time as native plants establish and become more abundant, and as lagged effects of historic agronomic disturbances abate. 

The benefits of prairie strips decreased with distance into cropland for spider abundance and richness, dung beetle abundance, active carbon, decomposition, and pollination (Figure 4). Each of these responses decreased with distance from the prairie strip, but did so by different mechanisms. For spiders, the spillover into cropland was delayed one year after the prairie strips were sown. Prairie strips provided new habitat and sources of prey for spiders (Hussain et al., 2021), such that spiders could move into cropland to capture additional prey. The impact on dung beetles and decomposition are likely due to the prairie strips harboring dung beetles in the year after restoration, which in turn caused a higher rate of manure removal near the prairie strips and a decrease in dung beetle abundance and manure removal with increasing distance from the strips (Manning and Cutler, 2018). For pollination, prairie strips increased floral resources which attracted pollinators and then exported them into the surrounding habitat (Garibaldi et al., 2011). We were surprised that prairie strips increased pollination as our plot sizes are a fraction of pollinator foraging range (Ricketts et al., 2008), and we suspect that pollinators were attracted to the high concentration of resources that contrasted strongly with crops.

Title: Flower strips as a carbon sequestration measure in temperate croplands
Snippet: For the first time, biomass of flower strips has been determined and analysed in relation to plant biodiversity. We found a significant negative correlation between the total number of unique plant species in the flower strip and its total biomass production, suggesting that highly diverse flower strips are less productive. The biomass of the flower strip is not harvested or removed, and thus flower strips have a much greater input of C to the soil compared to croplands. 

Additionally, the C sequestration potential of flower strips has also been modelled for the first time. We estimate that flower strips can sequester 0.48 Mg ± 0.36 C ha −1 year −1 in the initial 20 years after establishment in temperate, intensively used mineral soils. This rate is comparable to other C sequestrations methods, including cover crops and land use conversion to grassland. As with the total biomass, there is a negative correlation between C sequestration rate and biodiversity; thus there may be a trade-off between maximising plant biodiversity and C sequestration in flower strips. 

1 3 

Vol:. ( 1234567890) 

If an additional 1 % of German cropland on mineral soils was converted to flower strips, an additional 0.065 Tg C would be sequestered in the soil, which corresponds to 0.4 % of all GHG emissions from the German agricultural sector. Converting cropland to flower strips is not a fail-safe C sequestration method. Areas with already-high inputs of organic C from organic fertilisers, including manure, and biomass will see a lower potential C sequestering effect of flower strips. Furthermore, only a permanent flower strip can act as a significant C sink for climate mitigation. However, flower strips often improve agricultural yields through increased pollinator attraction and pest predation and have synergistic relations with overall ecosystem biodiversity. Therefore, implementing flower strips as a simple and easy-to-implement management option by farmers can improve multiple critical agro-environmental issues simultaneously.

Title: Prairie Strips and Lower Land Use Intensity Increase Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
Snippet: This conservation practice consists of retiring areas of farmland and actively restoring them by seeding native perennial vegetation. Supported by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) Conservation Reserve Program (CRP), prairie strips are one of many "edge of field" practices-including riparian buffers, hedgerows, and wildflower strips-aimed at incorporating native and diverse habitat into agricultural landscapes (The Nature Conservancy [TNC], 2021). 

Once established, prairie strips in contoured farm landscapes can reduce soil erosion, improve water quality, and support biodiversity. This can provide benefits to the farm and farmer at disproportionately higher levels than the amount of farmland removed from production (Schulte et al., 2017). Prairie strips also have the potential to provide resources and habitat for beneficial insects and increase their spillover into the farm, where they can provide ecosystem services such as biocontrol and pollination (Blitzer et al., 2012;Morandin and Kremen, 2013;Kordbacheh et al., 2020). While prairie strips are known to benefit biodiversity and ecosystem services once they have been established for multiple years, these impacts have not been studied during their initial years of establishment. Measuring prairie strips' conservation potential during their early establishment period can address this gap and increase the precision of farmers' expectations of prairie strips. 

The conservation potential of prairie strips relative to other agricultural conservation practices such as no tillage is also unknown. Biodiversity and ecosystem services in agroecosystems are driven not only by the presence of natural habitat on or near farms, but also by the agricultural management practices used in row crop areas. Crop rotations and cover crops generally increase biodiversity and enhance nutrient availability (Rusch et al., 2013;de Pedro et al., 2020;Bowers et al., 2021), whereas the use of tillage, pesticides, and fertilizer generally decrease biodiversity and increase greenhouse gas emissions (Syswerda and Robertson, 2014;Bowles et al., 2016;Raven and Wagner, 2021).
