attempts.answer:
Below we separate evidence on agrobiodiversity–stability relationships in Northern Great Plains (NGP) semi-arid cropping into (A) experimental manipulations that increase diversity (rotations/intercropping assigned to plots) and (B) observational comparisons of farmers and sites where stable moisture and low-disturbance histories favor adoption/sustenance of diverse systems. We then assess whether diversity drives stability or vice versa.

A. Experimental manipulations (rotation complexity, intercropping, and compatible-species sequences) and stability outcomes

Long-term, plot-level experiments in dryland systems show that rotations with more compatible, diverse species sequences—especially those incorporating legumes and varying rooting depth and resource use—produce higher average yields and more stable wheat production than monoculture or low-intensity rotations, with quantified reductions in the probability of low yields across years. <cite id="83f76394-1">Over 24 years in a dryland field in Colorado, rotations were ranked from most to least stable wheat production as: winter fallow no-till, winter fallow chisel, wheat–fallow, wheat–corn–millet–pea, wheat–corn–millet, wheat–corn–millet–fallow, wheat–millet, and wheat–continuous maize; wheat yields were highest when wheat followed fallow and lowest when wheat followed millet; the probability of producing below 1500 kg/ha was ~0.03 when wheat followed fallow but ~0.35–0.58 when wheat followed pea or millet, identifying an intensified wheat–millet–fallow rotation as relatively high-yield and stable</cite>. <cite id="1a97fd4f-0">Synthesis across dryland rotations in the western Central Great Plains shows that compatible-crop rotations (e.g., wheat with warm-season crops and legumes) consistently outperform monoculture, conferring yield advantages, pest/disease suppression, improved quality, reduced failure risk, and increased profit; common producer rotations are wheat–warm-season crop–fallow cycles, with two- to five-year sequences evaluated across crops including soybean, sunflower, sorghum, pulses, and alfalfa under dryland or limited irrigation</cite>.

Multi-year trials that explicitly integrate crop diversity and weather variability show that diversification reduces yield variability and failure risk, with effects strongest in unfavorable (hot/dry) years. <cite id="1a97fd4f-2">In a long-term corn–soybean trial, more diverse rotations significantly increased yield stability by mitigating hot/dry conditions; compared with more diverse sequences, corn–soybean monocultures had larger coefficients of variation, smaller cumulative and mean yields, and higher probabilities of low yields under unfavorable conditions; stability gains were particularly pronounced when legumes were included, with benefits varying by crop, weather, and tillage; the trial was conventionally managed to minimize confounding by organic system differences</cite>. <cite id="83f76394-0">At regional scale across the Great Plains, yield variability is high in states like North and South Dakota, and climate explains a notable share of yield variance in many counties, underscoring the value of management strategies that reduce temporal variability</cite>. Together, these manipulative experiments indicate that increasing rotation diversity via species complementarity and inclusion of nitrogen-fixing and moisture-use-diverse crops stabilizes wheat and corn production in semi-arid settings, especially during climatic stress.

No-till with diversified rotations is a second experimental pathway in NGP drylands that stabilizes output by improving moisture capture and suppressing weeds, enabling species portfolios that otherwise would fail under aridity. <cite id="189ea00c-0">Across NGP dryland systems, reduced tillage increases soil moisture retention and facilitates diversified rotations that include oilseeds, pulses, forages, and specialty crops; despite moisture constraints and warming trends, diversification and reduced disturbance have expanded conventional no-till dryland small-grain, pulse, and oilseed production in the region</cite>. <cite id="189ea00c-1">In western North Dakota and eastern Montana, no-till barley–pea rotations with adequate N fertilization achieved greater annualized grain yields than conventional-till systems while lowering net greenhouse gas potential and intensity, indicating robust management that sustains yields across differing soils and climates</cite>. These results show that management diversity (reduced disturbance + species diversity) reduces climatic sensitivity by conserving water and diversifying biotic functions, improving temporal stability of production.

B. Observational comparisons: farmers and sites with preexisting favorable conditions (stable moisture, low disturbance history) more likely to adopt/sustain diverse systems

At regional and county scales in the NGP, adoption patterns of diverse rotations and low disturbance align with moisture availability and risk/return considerations, implying reverse causality where stable sites attract diversification. <cite id="189ea00c-2">Between 1978 and 2012, crop diversity increased in central North Dakota (wetter subregion) but declined in eastern Dakotas; the expansion of no-till in central/western North Dakota conserved soil water, enabling broader crop species and reduced fallow in wheat/fallow rotations, likely helping control weeds and diseases; in contrast, eastern Dakotas with greater precipitation shifted toward corn and soybean specialization, illustrating how moisture stability and market/economic factors shape diversity patterns</cite>. <cite id="189ea00c-0">Historically, summer fallow conserved moisture and released nitrogen; more recently, reduced tillage has similarly conserved soil water and enabled diversification, yet terminal drought remains a key constraint, especially under warming scenarios, highlighting the interaction between climatic stability, disturbance history, and the feasibility of maintaining diverse rotations</cite>.

These observational patterns complement experimental findings by showing that where moisture is reliably available (e.g., drier central ND with adoption of no-till and diverse rotations, or wetter central ND where species breadth increased), farmers adopt and sustain diverse systems; conversely, where moisture variability and cooler, shorter growing conditions dominate, specialization (e.g., corn–soybean) increases, reducing diversity. <cite id="189ea00c-2">Spatial trends show more counties with low than high crop diversity and a downward trend in high-to-low cluster ratio in North Dakota, consistent with specialization pressures; analysis attributes increased diversity in central ND to no-till water conservation and diversification benefits, whereas eastern ND trends reflect genetic improvement and market gains for corn/soybean</cite>. Observational evidence also notes that longer/“compatible” rotations have been widely adopted in the region due to yield, pest suppression, and risk advantages, suggesting farmers’ choices respond to perceived stability and profit, not only to biodiversity per se. <cite id="1a97fd4f-0">Across multiple studies in the west-central Great Plains, rotations including wheat with warm-season crops and pulses were repeatedly shown to improve yield, suppress pests and diseases, and reduce failure risk, aligning with economic motivations that drive adoption</cite>.

C. Do diversity and stability go together? Experimental vs observational perspectives

Experiments in semi-arid cropping provide strong causal evidence that increasing diversity—through species-rich rotations, inclusion of legumes, and low disturbance/no-till—improves yield stability by mitigating climatic stress and reducing variance in production. <cite id="83f76394-1">A 24-year rotation comparison showed rotations with diversified sequences and reduced fallow frequency produced the most stable wheat outcomes and very low probabilities of low yields when wheat followed fallow; intensified rotations combining small grains with legumes and warm-season crops were notably stable</cite>. <cite id="1a97fd4f-2">Integrating corn and soybean into more diverse rotations significantly lowered variability and failure risk, especially under hot/dry conditions, with legume inclusion driving stability gains; because management differences were controlled, biological and functional diversity mechanisms are implicated</cite>. <cite id="189ea00c-1">No-till barley–pea rotations sustained yields and reduced net GHGs in dryland settings, indicating robustness across sites and soils when disturbance is minimized</cite>. These manipulations point to diversity as a driver of stability via functional complementarity, niche partitioning of resources (water, nitrogen), and suppression of pests and diseases, which collectively dampen year-to-year variability.

Observational studies, meanwhile, show that farmers’ portfolios and the landscape pattern of diversity covary with moisture stability and disturbance histories, indicating that stable sites and low-disturbance contexts are prerequisites for sustained diversity adoption. <cite id="189ea00c-2">Moisture-conserving no-till facilitated diversification in central/western North Dakota, whereas eastern ND adopted fewer diverse rotations, adopting corn/soybean due to improved genetics and economic returns; overall, more counties exhibit low crop diversity than high, consistent with specialization in risk-averse or moisture-limited settings</cite>. <cite id="189ea00c-0">In NGP drylands, fallow and reduced-till histories reflect attempts to manage moisture and nitrogen dynamics; however, rising temperatures and evapotranspiration increase terminal drought risk, complicating long-term sustainability of diversified systems unless moisture variability remains favorable</cite>.

Taken together, the direction of causality is bidirectional and context-dependent: diversity drives stability when mechanisms (functional complementarity, biological control, improved hydrologic use) are active in plot-scale experiments; stability (in moisture, soil structure, and disturbance history) drives adoption/sustenance of diverse systems at the farm and regional scales, where farmers select rotations that hedge climate and market risk. <cite id="1a97fd4f-0">Field rotations with compatible crops consistently reduce failure risk and improve yields and quality, aligning with observed regional adoption</cite>; <cite id="189ea00c-2">no-till-enabled moisture conservation and disease/weed cycle control in central ND allowed expansion of diverse rotations, while eastern ND moved toward monoculture specializations reflecting economic and climatic constraints</cite>.

D. Mechanisms and system-level pathways relevant to NGP semi-arid cropping

- Functional diversity and resource complementarity: rotations that combine small grains with warm-season crops, pulses, and forages exploit different rooting depths, phenologies, and water-use profiles, improving capture of rainfall and stored soil moisture and reducing within-season resource bottlenecks that elevate variability. <cite id="1a97fd4f-0">Compatible crops differ in water demand, rooting depth, allocate time to accumulate soil water, include nitrogen-fixers, and use resources across seasons, delivering yield advantage, pest suppression, and reduced failure risk</cite>.
- Disturbance and moisture conservation: reduced/no-till interacts synergistically with diversified rotations by increasing infiltration, soil water storage, and suppressing weeds, which lowers input risk and enables species that otherwise fail in semi-arid years. <cite id="189ea00c-0">Reduced tillage increases soil moisture retention and facilitates diversified rotations in NGP drylands</cite>; <cite id="189ea00c-1">barley–pea no-till rotations sustained yields while lowering net GHGs in western ND and eastern MT</cite>.
- Pest and disease dynamics: diversified rotations break pest cycles and reduce monoculture disease pressure, lowering the variance of harvest outcomes under climatic stress. <cite id="1a97fd4f-0">Rotations suppress crop pests and diseases, reducing failure risk</cite>.
- Weather insurance: diversity buffers against unfavorable extremes (hot/dry spells) by lowering sensitivity of crop physiological processes and supply-chain risks; experimental trials attribute stability gains in dry years to greater crop diversity, especially legume inclusion. <cite id="1a97fd4f-2">Yield stability significantly increased when corn and soybean were integrated into more diverse rotations, with clear benefits in dry years; previous observations were often confounded until controlled trials minimized management differences</cite>.

E. Implications and how to disentangle direction of effect in practice

For NGP semi-arid cropping, prioritize plot-scale, long-duration rotation trials and on-farm comparisons that manipulate diversity (sequence richness, legume inclusion, and reduced disturbance) while controlling for N management and pest pressure to quantify stability metrics (CV, low-yield probabilities, resilience) across moisture regimes. <cite id="83f76394-1">Long-running rotation experiments quantify stability across multiple measures and identify rotation sequences (e.g., wheat–fallow with legumes, intensified rotations) with low probabilities of low yield and high stability</cite>; <cite id="1a97fd4f-2">controlled, conventionally managed trials show diversity-driven stability increases, especially in hot/dry years</cite>. Complement with regional observations mapping adoption of diverse rotations to sites with long-term stable moisture (e.g., central ND with no-till and diversified rotations) and histories of low disturbance, versus moisture-limited or risk-averse areas favoring monoculture specializations. <cite id="189ea00c-2">Spatial analyses show no-till-enabled water conservation facilitated diversification in central ND, while eastern ND specialized in corn/soybean; overall, more counties exhibit low diversity than high</cite>.

In practice, diversity often drives stability when hydrologic and disturbance constraints are met; stable sites and practices (moisture conservation and low disturbance) enable sustained adoption and amplify diversity’s stabilizing effects. <cite id="83f76394-1">Diverse rotations with compatible species and reduced fallow frequency produced the most stable wheat outcomes</cite>; <cite id="189ea00c-0">reduced tillage in NGP drylands conserves moisture and enables diversified rotations</cite>; <cite id="189ea00c-2">adoption patterns reflect where moisture and disturbance histories allow diversification, and where risk/economics favor specialization</cite>.

Summary of relationships in NGP semi-arid cropping:

- Experimental manipulations (rotations with legumes and compatible species; no-till + diverse rotations) consistently increase yield stability and reduce low-yield risk, especially under hot/dry conditions, implying diversity drives stability via functional mechanisms. <cite id="83f76394-1">More diverse rotations increased stability and reduced the probability of low wheat yields; intensified rotations with legumes were highly stable</cite>; <cite id="1a97fd4f-2">integrating crops into more diverse rotations lowered variability and failure risk, particularly in dry years</cite>; <cite id="189ea00c-1">no-till barley–pea rotations sustained yields and reduced net GHGs across sites</cite>.
- Observational comparisons show farmers and regions with stable moisture and low disturbance histories are more likely to adopt and sustain diverse systems, while moisture-limited or risk-specialized areas exhibit lower diversity; this implies stability enables diversity adoption. <cite id="189ea00c-2">No-till water conservation facilitated diversification in central ND; eastern ND saw diversity declines with adoption of corn/soybean due to genetic and economic gains</cite>; <cite id="189ea00c-0">NGP dryland moisture constraints and warming trends complicate the sustainability of diversified systems unless disturbance is minimized and moisture variability is favorable</cite>.

Overall, both causal and correlational evidence converge: in NGP semi-arid systems, diversifying crop rotations and integrating legumes and low disturbance practices is an effective lever to improve agrobiodiversity–stability relationships, while stable moisture and low disturbance histories are enabling conditions for adoption. The strongest evidence for diversity→stability causality comes from long-term, controlled rotation trials and mechanistic attribution to weather shocks; stability→diversity evidence is strongest at regional scales where moisture reliability and tillage histories shape the distribution of diverse versus specialized systems. <cite id="83f76394-1">Rotational diversity and compatibility improved stability metrics and reduced low-yield risk</cite>; <cite id="1a97fd4f-2">diversity mitigated hot/dry stress and lowered yield variance</cite>; <cite id="189ea00c-0">reduced tillage conserved moisture and enabled diversification in NGP drylands</cite>; <cite id="189ea00c-2">spatial adoption patterns reflect moisture and disturbance histories as well as economic incentives</cite>.

Title: Wheat Yield and Yield Stability of Eight Dryland Crop Rotations
Snippet: The winter wheat (Triticum aestivum L.)–fallow (WF) dryland production system employed in the Central Great Plains has evolved in the past 40 yr to include a diversity of other crops, with a reduction in fallow frequency. Wheat remains the base crop for essentially all cropping systems. Decisions to change a farming system benefit from information about average wheat yields, yield stability, and probabilities of obtaining a specified minimum wheat yield. The objective of this experiment was to quantify wheat yields, yield stability, and the probability of obtaining a specified minimum yield in eight dryland rotational systems varying in cropping intensity. The study was conducted over a 24-yr period at Akron, CO. Yield stability was characterized with six stability measures. The probability of obtaining a yield less than 1500 kg ha⁻¹ was also calculated for each rotation. Wheat yields were greatest in rotations where wheat followed a fallow period and least where wheat followed millet production. Rotations ranked from most stable to least stable wheat production (averaged over the six stability measures) were WF(NT), WF(CT), WMF, WCMP, WCM, WCMF, WM, and WCF. The probability of producing <1500 kg ha⁻¹ was very low for rotations with wheat following fallow (about 0.03) and much higher for wheat following pea (0.35) or millet (0.48–0.58). The study results identified the WMF rotation as an intensified rotation with relatively high average wheat yields and yield stability.
</snippet>

Among the potential benefits of such a sustainable crop rotation is crop yield advantage (Sindelar et al., 2015;Schlegel et al., 2017), suppression of crop pest and disease (Holtzer et al., 1996;Derksen et al., 2002), increased quality (Havlin et al., 1990;Liebig et al., 2014), reduced risk of failure, and increased profit (Dhuyvetter et al., 1996;Williams et al., 2012).

In this region, the crop rotation commonly followed by producers is a winter wheat-warm season crop-fallow (W-Sc-F) rotation (Assefa et al., 2014;Hansen et al., 2012;Tarkalson et al., 2006). Title: Increasing Crop Diversity Mitigates Weather Variations and Improves Yield Stability
Snippet: Increasing rotation diversity improves yield stability by mitigating hot and dry weather and lowers risk of crop failure Compared to more diverse rotations, corn-soybean sequences had 1) larger coefficient of variations (Fig. 4); 2) smaller cumulative and mean yields over the course of the experiment (Table 1) and under various weather scenarios (Fig. 3, S5 Fig. ); and 3) higher probabilities of achieving low yields under unfavorable conditions (Table 2). Title: Organic Agriculture and the Quest for the Holy Grail in Water-Limited Ecosystems: Managing Weeds and Reducing Tillage Intensity
Snippet: The Northern Great Plains (NGP) is a vast prairie landscape in South Dakota, North Dakota, and Montana; parts of Northeastern Wyoming and Northwestern Nebraska; the arable regions of the Canadian provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta; and Northeastern British Columbia [8]. Traditionally, agriculture in the NGP has been based on drought-resistant crops such as spring wheat (Triticum aestivum L.), and summer fallow is commonly used to conserve soil moisture and release organic nitrogen (N). More recently, the adoption of reduced tillage systems in conventionally managed systems has increased soil moisture retention and facilitated diversified rotations that include oilseed, pulse, forage, and other specialty crops [9,10]. These advances have made the NGP one of the largest U.S. expanses of conventional no-till dryland small grain, pulse, and oilseed agriculture [11]. This region also has great potential for small grain organic production [9] and for low-intensity organic sheep production, as animals are raised on dry native range and can be finished on cover crops integrated with crop production [12][13][14]. Despite its potential, the challenges of organic agriculture in dryland agroecosystems are many. 

With a continental climate characterized by long, cold winters and short, warm summers, large diurnal ranges in temperature, strong winds, and variable and unpredictable precipitation [15], several environmental and biological factors hinder the sustainability of dryland organic agriculture across the NGP. First, in most years, soil moisture becomes depleted early in the summer and crops undergo terminal drought after anthesis, which reduces yield and impacts quality. This worrisome trend gets compounded as late winter/early spring temperatures have increased in the region since 1950 [16] and projections indicate that in areas within the NGP evapotranspiration constraints in mid-summer will increase [15], further increasing moisture challenges. It is predicted that the impacts of these new climate scenarios will become much more pronounced if temperatures rise above 31 • C and 35 • C during spring wheat anthesis and grain fill, respectively, or significant periods of unpredictable drought are experienced [17].
</snippet>

Below we separate evidence on agrobiodiversity–stability relationships in Northern Great Plains (NGP) semi-arid cropping into (A) experimental manipulations that increase diversity (rotations/intercropping assigned to plots) and (B) observational comparisons of farmers and sites where stable moisture and low-disturbance histories favor adoption/sustenance of diverse systems. We then assess whether diversity drives stability or vice versa.

A. Experimental manipulations (rotation complexity, intercropping, and compatible-species sequences) and stability outcomes

Long-term, plot-level experiments in dryland systems show that rotations with more compatible, diverse species sequences—especially those incorporating legumes and varying rooting depth and resource use—produce higher average yields and more stable wheat production than monoculture or low-intensity rotations, with quantified reductions in the probability of low yields across years. <cite id="83f76394-1">Over 24 years in a dryland field in Colorado, rotations were ranked from most to least stable wheat production as: winter fallow no-till, winter fallow chisel, wheat–fallow, wheat–corn–millet–pea, wheat–corn–millet, wheat–corn–millet–fallow, wheat–millet, and wheat–continuous maize; wheat yields were highest when wheat followed fallow and lowest when wheat followed millet; the probability of producing below 1500 kg/ha was ~0.03 when wheat followed fallow but ~0.35–0.58 when wheat followed pea or millet, identifying an intensified wheat–millet–fallow rotation as relatively high-yield and stable</cite>. <cite id="1a97fd4f-0">Synthesis across dryland rotations in the western Central Great Plains shows that compatible-crop rotations (e.g., wheat with warm-season crops and legumes) consistently outperform monoculture, conferring yield advantages, pest/disease suppression, improved quality, reduced failure risk, and increased profit; common producer rotations are wheat–warm-season crop–fallow cycles, with two- to five-year sequences evaluated across crops including soybean, sunflower, sorghum, pulses, and alfalfa under dryland or limited irrigation</cite>.

Multi-year trials that explicitly integrate crop diversity and weather variability show that diversification reduces yield variability and failure risk, with effects strongest in unfavorable (hot/dry) years. <cite id="1a97fd4f-2">In a long-term corn–soybean trial, more diverse rotations significantly increased yield stability by mitigating hot/dry conditions; compared with more diverse sequences, corn–soybean monocultures had larger coefficients of variation, smaller cumulative and mean yields, and higher probabilities of low yields under unfavorable conditions; stability gains were particularly pronounced when legumes were included, with benefits varying by crop, weather, and tillage; the trial was conventionally managed to minimize confounding by organic system differences</cite>. <cite id="83f76394-0">At regional scale across the Great Plains, yield variability is high in states like North and South Dakota, and climate explains a notable share of yield variance in many counties, underscoring the value of management strategies that reduce temporal variability</cite>. Together, these manipulative experiments indicate that increasing rotation diversity via species complementarity and inclusion of nitrogen-fixing and moisture-use-diverse crops stabilizes wheat and corn production in semi-arid settings, especially during climatic stress.

No-till with diversified rotations is a second experimental pathway in NGP drylands that stabilizes output by improving moisture capture and suppressing weeds, enabling species portfolios that otherwise would fail under aridity. <cite id="189ea00c-0">Across NGP dryland systems, reduced tillage increases soil moisture retention and facilitates diversified rotations that include oilseeds, pulses, forages, and specialty crops; despite moisture constraints and warming trends, diversification and reduced disturbance have expanded conventional no-till dryland small-grain, pulse, and oilseed production in the region</cite>. <cite id="189ea00c-1">In western North Dakota and eastern Montana, no-till barley–pea rotations with adequate N fertilization achieved greater annualized grain yields than conventional-till systems while lowering net greenhouse gas potential and intensity, indicating robust management that sustains yields across differing soils and climates</cite>. These results show that management diversity (reduced disturbance + species diversity) reduces climatic sensitivity by conserving water and diversifying biotic functions, improving temporal stability of production.

B. Observational comparisons: farmers and sites with preexisting favorable conditions (stable moisture, low disturbance history) more likely to adopt/sustain diverse systems

At regional and county scales in the NGP, adoption patterns of diverse rotations and low disturbance align with moisture availability and risk/return considerations, implying reverse causality where stable sites attract diversification. <cite id="189ea00c-2">Between 1978 and 2012, crop diversity increased in central North Dakota (wetter subregion) but declined in eastern Dakotas; the expansion of no-till in central/western North Dakota conserved soil water, enabling broader crop species and reduced fallow in wheat/fallow rotations, likely helping control weeds and diseases; in contrast, eastern Dakotas with greater precipitation shifted toward corn and soybean specialization, illustrating how moisture stability and market/economic factors shape diversity patterns</cite>. <cite id="189ea00c-0">Historically, summer fallow conserved moisture and released nitrogen; more recently, reduced tillage has similarly conserved soil water and enabled diversification, yet terminal drought remains a key constraint, especially under warming scenarios, highlighting the interaction between climatic stability, disturbance history, and the feasibility of maintaining diverse rotations</cite>.

These observational patterns complement experimental findings by showing that where moisture is reliably available (e.g., drier central ND with adoption of no-till and diverse rotations, or wetter central ND where species breadth increased), farmers adopt and sustain diverse systems; conversely, where moisture variability and cooler, shorter growing conditions dominate, specialization (e.g., corn–soybean) increases, reducing diversity. <cite id="189ea00c-2">Spatial trends show more counties with low than high crop diversity and a downward trend in high-to-low cluster ratio in North Dakota, consistent with specialization pressures; analysis attributes increased diversity in central ND to no-till water conservation and diversification benefits, whereas eastern ND trends reflect genetic improvement and market gains for corn/soybean</cite>. Observational evidence also notes that longer/“compatible” rotations have been widely adopted in the region due to yield, pest suppression, and risk advantages, suggesting farmers’ choices respond to perceived stability and profit, not only to biodiversity per se. <cite id="1a97fd4f-0">Across multiple studies in the west-central Great Plains, rotations including wheat with warm-season crops and pulses were repeatedly shown to improve yield, suppress pests and diseases, and reduce failure risk, aligning with economic motivations that drive adoption</cite>.

C. Do diversity and stability go together? Experimental vs observational perspectives

Experiments in semi-arid cropping provide strong causal evidence that increasing diversity—through species-rich rotations, inclusion of legumes, and low disturbance/no-till—improves yield stability by mitigating climatic stress and reducing variance in production. <cite id="83f76394-1">A 24-year rotation comparison showed rotations with diversified sequences and reduced fallow frequency produced the most stable wheat outcomes and very low probabilities of low yields when wheat followed fallow; intensified rotations combining small grains with legumes and warm-season crops were notably stable</cite>. <cite id="1a97fd4f-2">Integrating corn and soybean into more diverse rotations significantly lowered variability and failure risk, especially under hot/dry conditions, with legume inclusion driving stability gains; because management differences were controlled, biological and functional diversity mechanisms are implicated</cite>. <cite id="189ea00c-1">No-till barley–pea rotations sustained yields and reduced net GHGs in dryland settings, indicating robustness across sites and soils when disturbance is minimized</cite>. These manipulations point to diversity as a driver of stability via functional complementarity, niche partitioning of resources (water, nitrogen), and suppression of pests and diseases, which collectively dampen year-to-year variability.

Observational studies, meanwhile, show that farmers’ portfolios and the landscape pattern of diversity covary with moisture stability and disturbance histories, indicating that stable sites and low-disturbance contexts are prerequisites for sustained diversity adoption. <cite id="189ea00c-2">Moisture-conserving no-till facilitated diversification in central/western North Dakota, whereas eastern ND adopted fewer diverse rotations, adopting corn/soybean due to improved genetics and economic returns; overall, more counties exhibit low crop diversity than high, consistent with specialization in risk-averse or moisture-limited settings</cite>. <cite id="189ea00c-0">In NGP drylands, fallow and reduced-till histories reflect attempts to manage moisture and nitrogen dynamics; however, rising temperatures and evapotranspiration increase terminal drought risk, complicating long-term sustainability of diversified systems unless moisture variability remains favorable</cite>.

Taken together, the direction of causality is bidirectional and context-dependent: diversity drives stability when mechanisms (functional complementarity, biological control, improved hydrologic use) are active in plot-scale experiments; stability (in moisture, soil structure, and disturbance history) drives adoption/sustenance of diverse systems at the farm and regional scales, where farmers select rotations that hedge climate and market risk. <cite id="1a97fd4f-0">Field rotations with compatible crops consistently reduce failure risk and improve yields and quality, aligning with observed regional adoption</cite>; <cite id="189ea00c-2">no-till-enabled moisture conservation and disease/weed cycle control in central ND allowed expansion of diverse rotations, while eastern ND moved toward monoculture specializations reflecting economic and climatic constraints</cite>.

D. Mechanisms and system-level pathways relevant to NGP semi-arid cropping

- Functional diversity and resource complementarity: rotations that combine small grains with warm-season crops, pulses, and forages exploit different rooting depths, phenologies, and water-use profiles, improving capture of rainfall and stored soil moisture and reducing within-season resource bottlenecks that elevate variability. <cite id="1a97fd4f-0">Compatible crops differ in water demand, rooting depth, allocate time to accumulate soil water, include nitrogen-fixers, and use resources across seasons, delivering yield advantage, pest suppression, and reduced failure risk</cite>.
- Disturbance and moisture conservation: reduced/no-till interacts synergistically with diversified rotations by increasing infiltration, soil water storage, and suppressing weeds, which lowers input risk and enables species that otherwise fail in semi-arid years. <cite id="189ea00c-0">Reduced tillage increases soil moisture retention and facilitates diversified rotations in NGP drylands</cite>; <cite id="189ea00c-1">barley–pea no-till rotations sustained yields while lowering net GHGs in western ND and eastern MT</cite>.
- Pest and disease dynamics: diversified rotations break pest cycles and reduce monoculture disease pressure, lowering the variance of harvest outcomes under climatic stress. <cite id="1a97fd4f-0">Rotations suppress crop pests and diseases, reducing failure risk</cite>.
- Weather insurance: diversity buffers against unfavorable extremes (hot/dry spells) by lowering sensitivity of crop physiological processes and supply-chain risks; experimental trials attribute stability gains in dry years to greater crop diversity, especially legume inclusion. <cite id="1a97fd4f-2">Yield stability significantly increased when corn and soybean were integrated into more diverse rotations, with clear benefits in dry years; previous observations were often confounded until controlled trials minimized management differences</cite>.

E. Implications and how to disentangle direction of effect in practice

For NGP semi-arid cropping, prioritize plot-scale, long-duration rotation trials and on-farm comparisons that manipulate diversity (sequence richness, legume inclusion, and reduced disturbance) while controlling for N management and pest pressure to quantify stability metrics (CV, low-yield probabilities, resilience) across moisture regimes. <cite id="83f76394-1">Long-running rotation experiments quantify stability across multiple measures and identify rotation sequences (e.g., wheat–fallow with legumes, intensified rotations) with low probabilities of low yield and high stability</cite>; <cite id="1a97fd4f-2">controlled, conventionally managed trials show diversity-driven stability increases, especially in hot/dry years</cite>. Complement with regional observations mapping adoption of diverse rotations to sites with long-term stable moisture (e.g., central ND with no-till and diversified rotations) and histories of low disturbance, versus moisture-limited or risk-averse areas favoring monoculture specializations. <cite id="189ea00c-2">Spatial analyses show no-till-enabled water conservation facilitated diversification in central ND, while eastern ND specialized in corn/soybean; overall, more counties exhibit low diversity than high</cite>.

In practice, diversity often drives stability when hydrologic and disturbance constraints are met; stable sites and practices (moisture conservation and low disturbance) enable sustained adoption and amplify diversity’s stabilizing effects. <cite id="83f76394-1">Diverse rotations with compatible species and reduced fallow frequency produced the most stable wheat outcomes</cite>; <cite id="189ea00c-0">reduced tillage in NGP drylands conserves moisture and enables diversified rotations</cite>; <cite id="189ea00c-2">adoption patterns reflect where moisture and disturbance histories allow diversification, and where risk/economics favor specialization</cite>.

Summary of relationships in NGP semi-arid cropping:

- Experimental manipulations (rotations with legumes and compatible species; no-till + diverse rotations) consistently increase yield stability and reduce low-yield risk, especially under hot/dry conditions, implying diversity drives stability via functional mechanisms. <cite id="83f76394-1">More diverse rotations increased stability and reduced the probability of low wheat yields; intensified rotations with legumes were highly stable</cite>; <cite id="1a97fd4f-2">integrating crops into more diverse rotations lowered variability and failure risk, particularly in dry years</cite>; <cite id="189ea00c-1">no-till barley–pea rotations sustained yields and reduced net GHGs across sites</cite>.
- Observational comparisons show farmers and regions with stable moisture and low disturbance histories are more likely to adopt and sustain diverse systems, while moisture-limited or risk-specialized areas exhibit lower diversity; this implies stability enables diversity adoption. <cite id="189ea00c-2">No-till water conservation facilitated diversification in central ND; eastern ND saw diversity declines with adoption of corn/soybean due to genetic and economic gains</cite>; <cite id="189ea00c-0">NGP dryland moisture constraints and warming trends complicate the sustainability of diversified systems unless disturbance is minimized and moisture variability is favorable</cite>.

Overall, both causal and correlational evidence converge: in NGP semi-arid systems, diversifying crop rotations and integrating legumes and low disturbance practices is an effective lever to improve agrobiodiversity–stability relationships, while stable moisture and low disturbance histories are enabling conditions for adoption. The strongest evidence for diversity→stability causality comes from long-term, controlled rotation trials and mechanistic attribution to weather shocks; stability→diversity evidence is strongest at regional scales where moisture reliability and tillage histories shape the distribution of diverse versus specialized systems. <cite id="83f76394-1">Rotational diversity and compatibility improved stability metrics and reduced low-yield risk</cite>; <cite id="1a97fd4f-2">diversity mitigated hot/dry stress and lowered yield variance</cite>; <cite id="189ea00c-0">reduced tillage conserved moisture and enabled diversification in NGP drylands</cite>; <cite id="189ea00c-2">spatial adoption patterns reflect moisture and disturbance histories as well as economic incentives</cite>. </answer>

Title: Climate-Driven Crop Yield and Yield Variability and Climate Change Impacts on the U.S. Great Plains Agricultural Production
Snippet: This study builds upon a comprehensive approach to realize the impacts of climate variability on crop yields and production by addressing a series of constituent questions in a stepwise fashion. Crop yields were studied to discover the trends and inter-annual variability during the 4.6 decades period over the Great Plains region. A key observation was high CV in crop yields for some regions such as North Dakota and South Dakota, which point towards the facts that areas with lower yields or less contribution to regional production demonstrate higher inter-annual variation than the key producing regions such as Nebraska, Kansas, and Iowa. This finding has also been reported on U.S. national and global scales, respectively 18,21 . Overall, soybean yields exhibited lowest variability relative to maize and sorghum. Leng et al. 18 showed that similar spatial patterns exist in maize and soybean yield variability in the Great Plains region, although their analyses differed from ours in terms of: (a) the use of standard deviation to interpret crop yield variability, and (b) the period of analyses (1983-2012). Stability in crop yields is important, especially now than ever, when demands for food, feed, and fiber are increasing 22 due to rapidly growing global population, and productivity rates have been lagging 23 . Crop yield variability, and hence variability in production, can affect national food stocks, spikes in food prices, and the livelihood of the citizens and other stakeholders involved. Therefore, the regions which contribute largely to national production should ideally be more resilient to variability to avoid these ramifications as even small levels of variability can affect productivity drastically. At the same time, greater variability in the regions of less consequence to regional or national production, would result in similar impacts in the local food availability scenario of these regions. Hence, our efforts to quantify crop yield variability in this study generate critical information on the state of these regions in the context of food security and quantitatively emphasizes that regions differ in their susceptibility to factors that can affect crop yields. 

Further, we establish how much of the crop yield variability is explained by climate and its dynamics across the spatial domain. We found that there was considerable number of counties where climate explained more than 20% of the crop yield variability.

Title: Wheat Yield and Yield Stability of Eight Dryland Crop Rotations
Snippet: The winter wheat (Triticum aestivum L.)–fallow (WF) dryland production system employed in the Central Great Plains has evolved in the past 40 yr to include a diversity of other crops, with a reduction in fallow frequency. Wheat remains the base crop for essentially all cropping systems. Decisions to change a farming system benefit from information about average wheat yields, yield stability, and probabilities of obtaining a specified minimum wheat yield. The objective of this experiment was to quantify wheat yields, yield stability, and the probability of obtaining a specified minimum yield in eight dryland rotational systems varying in cropping intensity. The study was conducted over a 24-yr period at Akron, CO. Yield stability was characterized with six stability measures. The probability of obtaining a yield less than 1500 kg ha⁻¹ was also calculated for each rotation. Wheat yields were greatest in rotations where wheat followed a fallow period and least where wheat followed millet production. Rotations ranked from most stable to least stable wheat production (averaged over the six stability measures) were WF(NT), WF(CT), WMF, WCMP, WCM, WCMF, WM, and WCF. The probability of producing <1500 kg ha⁻¹ was very low for rotations with wheat following fallow (about 0.03) and much higher for wheat following pea (0.35) or millet (0.48–0.58). The study results identified the WMF rotation as an intensified rotation with relatively high average wheat yields and yield stability.

Title: Yield and Overall Productivity under Long-Term Wheat-Based Crop Rotations: 2000 through 2016
Snippet: otation of compatible crops is a consistently proven sustainable dryland cropping system in semiarid regions compared with monocropping (Van Duivenbooden et al., 2000;Davis et al., 2012;Nielsen and Vigil, 2018). Compatible crops in rotation often have varying water demand, different rooting depth, enough time between harvesting of one crop to planting date of the next crop to accumulate soil water, include crops that are able to fix nitrogen, use resources in different parts of the season, and/or other traits (Nielsen et al., 2011). Among the potential benefits of such a sustainable crop rotation is crop yield advantage (Sindelar et al., 2015;Schlegel et al., 2017), suppression of crop pest and disease (Holtzer et al., 1996;Derksen et al., 2002), increased quality (Havlin et al., 1990;Liebig et al., 2014), reduced risk of failure, and increased profit (Dhuyvetter et al., 1996;Williams et al., 2012). 

In the west-central Great Plains; corn (C), grain sorghum (GS), soybean (SB), sunflower (SF), and winter wheat (W) are the dominant dryland crops. In this region, the crop rotation commonly followed by producers is a winter wheat-warm season crop-fallow (W-Sc-F) rotation (Assefa et al., 2014;Hansen et al., 2012;Tarkalson et al., 2006). Various two-to five-year cycled rotation systems were evaluated by different researchers (Anderson et al., 1999;Wright and Anderson, 2000;Williams et al., 2012;Nielsen and Vigil, 2014;Schlegel et al., 2016a;Schlegel et al., 2017). Crops included in these studies were W, C, GS, SF, SB, proso millet (M, Panicum miliaceum L.), field pea (P, Pisum sativum L.) or forage [such as alfalfa (Medicago sativa L).] either in dryland or limited irrigation conditions.

Title: Increasing Crop Diversity Mitigates Weather Variations and Improves Yield Stability
Snippet: Increasing rotation diversity improves yield stability by mitigating hot and dry weather and lowers risk of crop failure Compared to more diverse rotations, corn-soybean sequences had 1) larger coefficient of variations (Fig. 4); 2) smaller cumulative and mean yields over the course of the experiment (Table 1) and under various weather scenarios (Fig. 3, S5 Fig. ); and 3) higher probabilities of achieving low yields under unfavorable conditions (Table 2). Although the magnitude of rotation benefits varied with crops, weather patterns and tillage (Fig. 3), yield stability significantly increased when corn and soybean were integrated into more diverse rotations, especially when legumes were introduced (Fig. 3, Fig. 4). Our findings of increased yield stability support the conclusions of previous studies showing that longer or more diverse rotations improve the temporal stability of grain yields [33,36,37,39,[55][56][57]. 

Resilience is rooted in the concept of stability, and describes how a system responds under stress [17]. Our study does not investigate systems response to stress during crop development and fluctuations in crop physiological and yield potential status during stress would have to be studied to clearly establish how crop diversity and tillage alter the dynamic of crop stability (ie: resilience, tolerance, resistance). By emphasizing adaptive management strategies, resilience thinking has been proposed as a new way to inform the changes in practices necessary to adapt cropping systems to shifts in resource availability [58]. Future studies are necessary to examine both spatial and temporal aspects of resilience applied to cropping systems. 

We clearly show that the effects of crop diversity vary with weather conditions and conclusively attribute larger yield stability in dry years to greater crop diversity (Figs. 3, 4). Previous observations of rotation benefits in droughty or low-yielding environments were often anecdotal or confounded by management practice differences across organic and conventional systems [5,33,34,36,37,39,40,59,60]. Our trial was conventionally managed, with similar fertilizer regime and pest pressure between plots and no effects of such factors on productivity.

Increasing rotation diversity improves yield stability by mitigating hot and dry weather and lowers risk of crop failure Compared to more diverse rotations, corn-soybean sequences had 1) larger coefficient of variations (Fig. 4); 2) smaller cumulative and mean yields over the course of the experiment (Table 1) and under various weather scenarios (Fig. 3, S5 Fig. ); and 3) higher probabilities of achieving low yields under unfavorable conditions (Table 2). Although the magnitude of rotation benefits varied with crops, weather patterns and tillage (Fig. 3), yield stability significantly increased when corn and soybean were integrated into more diverse rotations, especially when legumes were introduced (Fig. 3, Fig. 4). Our findings of increased yield stability support the conclusions of previous studies showing that longer or more diverse rotations improve the temporal stability of grain yields [33,36,37,39,[55][56][57]. 

Resilience is rooted in the concept of stability, and describes how a system responds under stress [17]. Our study does not investigate systems response to stress during crop development and fluctuations in crop physiological and yield potential status during stress would have to be studied to clearly establish how crop diversity and tillage alter the dynamic of crop stability (ie: resilience, tolerance, resistance). By emphasizing adaptive management strategies, resilience thinking has been proposed as a new way to inform the changes in practices necessary to adapt cropping systems to shifts in resource availability [58]. Future studies are necessary to examine both spatial and temporal aspects of resilience applied to cropping systems. 

We clearly show that the effects of crop diversity vary with weather conditions and conclusively attribute larger yield stability in dry years to greater crop diversity (Figs. 3, 4). Previous observations of rotation benefits in droughty or low-yielding environments were often anecdotal or confounded by management practice differences across organic and conventional systems [5,33,34,36,37,39,40,59,60]. Our trial was conventionally managed, with similar fertilizer regime and pest pressure between plots and no effects of such factors on productivity.

documents.title: Yield and Overall Productivity under Long-Term Wheat-Based Crop Rotations: 2000 through 2016
documents.snippet:
otation of compatible crops is a consistently proven sustainable dryland cropping system in semiarid regions compared with monocropping (Van Duivenbooden et al., 2000;Davis et al., 2012;Nielsen and Vigil, 2018). Compatible crops in rotation often have varying water demand, different rooting depth, enough time between harvesting of one crop to planting date of the next crop to accumulate soil water, include crops that are able to fix nitrogen, use resources in different parts of the season, and/or other traits (Nielsen et al., 2011). Among the potential benefits of such a sustainable crop rotation is crop yield advantage (Sindelar et al., 2015;Schlegel et al., 2017), suppression of crop pest and disease (Holtzer et al., 1996;Derksen et al., 2002), increased quality (Havlin et al., 1990;Liebig et al., 2014), reduced risk of failure, and increased profit (Dhuyvetter et al., 1996;Williams et al., 2012). 

In the west-central Great Plains; corn (C), grain sorghum (GS), soybean (SB), sunflower (SF), and winter wheat (W) are the dominant dryland crops. In this region, the crop rotation commonly followed by producers is a winter wheat-warm season crop-fallow (W-Sc-F) rotation (Assefa et al., 2014;Hansen et al., 2012;Tarkalson et al., 2006). Various two-to five-year cycled rotation systems were evaluated by different researchers (Anderson et al., 1999;Wright and Anderson, 2000;Williams et al., 2012;Nielsen and Vigil, 2014;Schlegel et al., 2016a;Schlegel et al., 2017). Crops included in these studies were W, C, GS, SF, SB, proso millet (M, Panicum miliaceum L.), field pea (P, Pisum sativum L.) or forage [such as alfalfa (Medicago sativa L).] either in dryland or limited irrigation conditions.

documents.title: Wheat Yield and Yield Stability of Eight Dryland Crop Rotations
documents.snippet: The winter wheat (Triticum aestivum L.)–fallow (WF) dryland production system employed in the Central Great Plains has evolved in the past 40 yr to include a diversity of other crops, with a reduction in fallow frequency. Wheat remains the base crop for essentially all cropping systems. Decisions to change a farming system benefit from information about average wheat yields, yield stability, and probabilities of obtaining a specified minimum wheat yield. The objective of this experiment was to quantify wheat yields, yield stability, and the probability of obtaining a specified minimum yield in eight dryland rotational systems varying in cropping intensity. The study was conducted over a 24-yr period at Akron, CO. Yield stability was characterized with six stability measures. The probability of obtaining a yield less than 1500 kg ha⁻¹ was also calculated for each rotation. Wheat yields were greatest in rotations where wheat followed a fallow period and least where wheat followed millet production. Rotations ranked from most stable to least stable wheat production (averaged over the six stability measures) were WF(NT), WF(CT), WMF, WCMP, WCM, WCMF, WM, and WCF. The probability of producing <1500 kg ha⁻¹ was very low for rotations with wheat following fallow (about 0.03) and much higher for wheat following pea (0.35) or millet (0.48–0.58). The study results identified the WMF rotation as an intensified rotation with relatively high average wheat yields and yield stability.

Title: Organic Agriculture and the Quest for the Holy Grail in Water-Limited Ecosystems: Managing Weeds and Reducing Tillage Intensity
Snippet: The Northern Great Plains (NGP) is a vast prairie landscape in South Dakota, North Dakota, and Montana; parts of Northeastern Wyoming and Northwestern Nebraska; the arable regions of the Canadian provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta; and Northeastern British Columbia [8]. Traditionally, agriculture in the NGP has been based on drought-resistant crops such as spring wheat (Triticum aestivum L.), and summer fallow is commonly used to conserve soil moisture and release organic nitrogen (N). More recently, the adoption of reduced tillage systems in conventionally managed systems has increased soil moisture retention and facilitated diversified rotations that include oilseed, pulse, forage, and other specialty crops [9,10]. These advances have made the NGP one of the largest U.S. expanses of conventional no-till dryland small grain, pulse, and oilseed agriculture [11]. This region also has great potential for small grain organic production [9] and for low-intensity organic sheep production, as animals are raised on dry native range and can be finished on cover crops integrated with crop production [12][13][14]. Despite its potential, the challenges of organic agriculture in dryland agroecosystems are many. 

With a continental climate characterized by long, cold winters and short, warm summers, large diurnal ranges in temperature, strong winds, and variable and unpredictable precipitation [15], several environmental and biological factors hinder the sustainability of dryland organic agriculture across the NGP. First, in most years, soil moisture becomes depleted early in the summer and crops undergo terminal drought after anthesis, which reduces yield and impacts quality. This worrisome trend gets compounded as late winter/early spring temperatures have increased in the region since 1950 [16] and projections indicate that in areas within the NGP evapotranspiration constraints in mid-summer will increase [15], further increasing moisture challenges. It is predicted that the impacts of these new climate scenarios will become much more pronounced if temperatures rise above 31 • C and 35 • C during spring wheat anthesis and grain fill, respectively, or significant periods of unpredictable drought are experienced [17].
